articles.title: Goodram Expands Its Gaming-Focused RIVAL Series With RIVAL Charge DDR5 Memory
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 22nd 2026
	
	
	
	
Goodram Expands Its Gaming-Focused RIVAL Series With RIVAL Charge DDR5 Memory
Goodram is expanding its gaming-focused RIVAL series with RIVAL Charge DDR5 memory. The new DIMM modules are designed for computers based on DDR5 platforms, including both new systems and upgraded configurations. The series includes variants with speeds of up to 6800 MT/s and latencies starting from CL30, as well as kits with a total capacity of up to 64 GB.
Gaming today is about more than just the game
A game, Discord, a browser with multiple tabs, gameplay recording, streaming and system monitoring—in a modern gaming configuration, RAM rarely serves just one application.RIVAL Charge DDR5 was designed with exactly this kind of workload in mind. Higher memory bandwidth is beneficial when multiple operations are running in parallel, while the right capacity gives the system more headroom when several demanding applications are active at the same time.
That is why RIVAL Charge lets users choose not only the frequency and latency, but also the capacity that best reflects how the computer is actually used.
6800 MT/s makes an impression. But it is not the only number that matters
When choosing DDR5 memory, it is easy to focus primarily on frequency. However, the MT/s figure alone does not tell the whole story about a module's performance characteristics. Latency, specified among others by CAS Latency (CL), is equally important. RIVAL Charge will be available in 5600 and 6000 MT/s configurations with latencies starting from CL30, 6400 MT/s CL32, and 6800 MT/s CL34. Selected CL36 variants will also be available.
This broad range makes it possible to match the memory to the capabilities of the processor and motherboard instead of reducing the choice to the highest available MT/s value. When building a computer, the entire set of parameters matters—speed, latency, compatibility and capacity.
The capacity range is equally broad. RIVAL Charge will be available as individual 8, 16 and 32 GB modules, as well as dual-channel kits: 2 × 8 GB, 2 × 16 GB and 2 × 32 GB. This makes it possible to build configurations ranging from 16 GB for less demanding systems, through a versatile 32 GB for gaming and multitasking, up to 64 GB for users who game, stream, edit content or work with more demanding applications on the same computer.
DDR5 for where a new configuration begins
RIVAL Charge expands the Goodram RIVAL family with a solution designed for DDR5 platforms. Existing RIVAL DDR4 modules remain an option for users upgrading computers based on the older standard without having to replace the processor and motherboard.
RIVAL Charge, on the other hand, is aimed at new and upgraded configurations using DDR5. The range from 5600 to 6800 MT/s makes it possible to choose memory for both more straightforward gaming PCs and higher-performance systems also used for streaming or content creation.Profiles instead of manual parameter tuning
RIVAL Charge supports Intel XMP 3.0 and AMD EXPO profiles. On a compatible platform, they allow users to apply predefined frequency, latency and voltage settings without having to configure each parameter manually.
After selecting the appropriate profile in the BIOS, the user can activate settings prepared for a specific memory variant. This is particularly useful for those who want to take advantage of the modules' capabilities without manually configuring individual DRAM parameters.
Red is only the beginning
The first RIVAL Charge modules feature a red-and-black heat spreader and a black PCB, maintaining the distinctive gaming aesthetic of the RIVAL family. This color variant is only the beginning, however—Goodram plans to expand the RIVAL Charge line with additional color options, giving users greater freedom to match the memory to the overall look of their system.
This is particularly relevant in computers where components increasingly form part of the visual design—from the color of the case and cooling system to the motherboard, cables and other components. Design, however, does not come at the expense of compatibility. The modules are 32.85 mm high, and their low-profile design makes them easier to use in configurations with larger CPU coolers, where space above the DIMM slots may be limited.
Like other Goodram RIVAL memory modules, RIVAL Charge DDR5 is covered by the manufacturer's lifetime warranty.

articles.title: Dyson’s most overengineered gadget may have a waterproofing problem
articles.text:
There’s always a danger in over-complicating products. Simple is so often best. The apocryphal story of NASA spending millions crafting a space pen while Soviet cosmonauts used a pencil is often cited as a prime example, even if it’s actually not true. Perhaps it’s not surprising that Dyson has got into hot water trying to reinvent the electric toothbrush.
The Chinese invented the first bristle toothbrush during the Ming dynasty. That concept muddled along quite nicely until 1937, when Tomlinson Moseley filed a patent for the earliest electric toothbrush. After more than 400 years, the Motodent marked the beginning of an evolutionary shift from manual brushing to powered oral care.
Having had considerable success reimagining established product categories such as stick vacuums and premium hair dryers—though not so much air-purifying headphones—the company earlier this month, with great fanfare, unveiled the next leap forward for teeth: the $499 Dyson CameraJet with a tiny camera to aim streams of rinsing fluid into the gaps between your teeth.
Others, like the Waterpik Sonic-Fusion 2.0, have already been daring (or foolhardy) enough to combine brushing and water flossing. However, Dyson upped the ante further by adding a macro-lens camera, allowing its “Gap Optical Targeting system,” trained on 470,000 dental images, to identify within 100 milliseconds precisely where to squirt fluid from the 12.5 milliliters of mouth rinse stored in its on-board reservoir.
It’s taken Dyson six years, 38 patents, and an awful lot of money to make this camera-squirt-brush doohickey work. However, something has gone badly wrong with the CameraJet. So wrong that despite James Dyson globally launching the product at a Paris event mere weeks ago, you can no longer, as far as WIRED can ascertain, buy the CameraJet anywhere.
The CameraJet launched in US stores on September 8. Just a day later, reports began outlining the first user complaints of water in the battery compartment and failures within 30 seconds of use. Consumer Reports’ own review unit stopped working less than 24 hours after unboxing. On September 11, French outlet Numerama reported that the French Dyson site and stores had reportedly stopped selling the toothbrush. By September 15, stores in the US, UK, and Singapore, where Dyson’s headquarters now reside, had followed suit.

articles.title: Como medir a distância entre dois pontos no Google Maps • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Como medir a distância entre dois pontos no Google Maps
O medidor de distância do Google Maps é usado para descobrir o quão longe ou quão perto estão dois endereços em linha reta
Medir a distância no Google Maps é um recurso que permite estimar a proximidade entre locais. A ferramenta calcula em linha reta a extensão de terrenos, bairros e até mesmo a distância entre cidades, sem limitar-se aos trajetos de ruas.
Para utilizar a função, basta selecionar um ponto neutro no mapa e selecionar a opção de medição para escolher o segundo local. Então, o aplicativo ou a página do Google Maps calcula a distância entre os pontos e apresenta a medida estimada entre eles.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te mostra como medir a distância no Google Maps no Android, iPhone e PC.
Abra o Google Maps no celular Android ou iPhone e mantenha o dedo pressionado sobre uma área neutra no mapa até aparecer um alfinete vermelho.
Importante: evite tocar em nomes de estabelecimentos ou pontos de interesse já cadastrados, pois essa opção não aparece na ficha comercial desses locais.
Arraste para cima a ficha do local marcado na parte inferior da tela e toque em “Medir distância”. Uma linha pontilhada com um ponto de mira será ativada na tela para você medir a distância no Google Maps do celular.
Mova o mapa para posicionar a linha sobre o destino desejado e toque em “Adicionar”, no canto inferior direito. Então, o Google Maps exibirá a distância entre dois endereços na parte inferior esquerda da tela.
Use o navegador do seu PC para acessar maps.google.com.
Clique com o botão direito do mouse sobre o local onde deseja iniciar a medição e selecione a opção “Medir distância”.
Importante: prefira clicar em uma área neutra do mapa, evitando estabelecimentos ou pontos turísticos que exibem fichas comerciais.
Clique com o botão esquerdo do mouse sobre o segundo local para calcular a distância no Google Maps.
Por fim, veja os dados da distância entre os endereços no menu localizado na parte inferior da tela do Google Maps.
O medidor de distância do Google Maps exige condições específicas para aparecer no menu, seja no navegador ou nos dispositivos móveis. Estes são alguns dos motivos que impedem o uso da ferramenta:
Medir a distância no Google Maps calcula a separação geométrica em linha reta, sem considerar ruas, trânsito ou vias urbanas. Trata-se de uma ferramenta de medição espacial voltada para estimar a proximidade física direta entre dois locais de forma simples.
Traçar uma rota no Google Maps, por sua vez, gera um trajeto navegável integrado à malha viária, adaptado ao modo de transporte escolhido, como carro, caminhada ou transporte público. Esse recurso calcula a distância e o tempo de deslocamento, oferecendo um caminho otimizado para navegação.

articles.title: Bambu Lab R1 Review: This one stands alone
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
Great hardware combined with Bambu’s excellent software and smooth user interface puts this laser among the best. The 55W CO2 laser cutter and engraver makes quick work of wood, acrylic, glass, and more.
Pros
- +Easy to assemble
- +Simple to calibrate
- +Great camera accuracy
- +Smaller footprint than other lasers in its class
- +Bambu Suite software
- +Great price
Cons
- -Optional lens required for thicker material
- -Limited material presets listed
- -Loud fans
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Bambu Lab has swung for the fences with its second go at making a laser cutter, and this time, it knocked it out of the park. The Bambu Lab R1 is a standalone, 55W CO2 laser with a roomy 600 x 300 mm work area, a bird’s eye camera for remote positioning, and a well-designed software suite. Priced at $2,499, the laser is a steal compared to other CO2 lasers of the same size and caliber.
You might recall the company’s first laser, a 40w diode packaged inside the H2D, was met with skepticism. Though the company pitched the H2D as the ultimate mini manufacturing machine for makers, many people felt a laser was too dirty to house in the same box as an expensive Core XY printer. Bambu must be listening, because they took everything that was good about the H2D’s diode system and gave it a standalone case with a massive CO2 laser.
The R1 has the same simple unboxing and setup experience as a Bambu Lab printer, making it easy to get started without a ton of prior experience. The only thing it is currently lacking is a more comprehensive set of material presets. Bambu Suite really shines in a market where good hardware is often let down by bad software.
While the Bambu Lab R1 is not a small machine, it does have a smaller footprint than other lasers with a similar work area. It requires a stout work table – and two people to cart it into position – as the machine is over 70 pounds. In its base configuration the R1 has a work area of 600mm x 300mm. With the optional conveyor and riser base, that 300mm can be extended to 3000mm, or 9.8 feet. Of course, you’ll need a lot of space in front of and behind the machine to pull that off. Bambu Lab did a wonderful job putting all of the controls and frequently used ports near the front of the R1 since you won’t want to move it much unless you are lasering something large.
The only flaw I found was the need to manually change focus lenses to cut thicker material. The process to change lenses is tedious, with six screws needing to be removed and replaced with the new lens. The two screws for the toolhead cover are ridiculously small. This process is reminiscent of the early Bambu Lab printer nozzles that required the heater and thermistor to be detached, then reinstalled with thermal paste. Hopefully Bambu Lab will come up with a quick-release lens at some point in the future.
Specifications: Bambu Lab R1
| Machine Footprint | 940 x 560 x 200 mm (37 x 22 x 7.8 inches) | 
| Machine Weight | 33.5 kg (73.8 lbs) | 
| Engraving Size | 600 x 300 mm (23.6 x 11.8 inches) With Conveyor 600 x 3000 mm (23.6 x 118.1 inches) | 
| Material | Cuts wood, acrylic (incl. clear acrylic), leather, fabric, paper, EVA foam, and shell. | 
| Engraves | The above plus coated metal, glass, and ceramic | 
| Laser Type | CO2 | 
| Laser Power | 55W | 
| Laser Wave Length | 10600 nm | 
| Engraving Accuracy | 0.10 mm | 
| Cutting Platform | Metal slats and baseplate included | 
| Connectivity | USB, Wi-Fi | 
| Interface | Color touch screen | 
| MSRP | $2,499 | 
| Release Date | September 22, 2026 | 
Bambu Lab R1: Included in the Box
The Bambu Lab R1 arrives fully assembled with its accessory pack bundled inside the laser enclosure. Accessories include a tool kit, exhaust hose, ventilation fan, antifreeze, funnel, laser alignment sensor, calibration board, and a material pack of basswood plywood and clear acrylic. You will need to supply 1500ml of distilled water to dilute the antifreeze. For the review, we also received the medium and long focus lenses, the conveyor and the riser needed for its use, the auto fire extinguishing system, and a smoke purifier.
Design of the Bambu Lab R1
The Bambu Lab R1 is a beast of a machine, but a well-thought-out one. It’s more compact than other CO2 lasers with the same working area, despite this, weighing over 70lbs. It’s not an easy machine to move. Bambu Lab put all of the controls, ports, and the safety key thoughtfully within easy reach at the front of the machine. The color touchscreen and start button are on top of the machine.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The automatic fire extinguisher ports, USB-C, and safety key are located on the left side of the laser.
The emergency stop button is located on the right side of the laser.
Only the power switch, the exhaust fan, and the coolant filling point are located on the rear of the unit.
Unlike most other lasers, a CO2 laser has a large, glass, liquid-cooled laser tube at the rear of the unit. Antifreeze is mixed with distilled water for the coolant to prevent the glass tube from freezing should it be kept in a garage, basement or even if you lose power in your house during the winter.
The laser fires a beam which is directed to the tool head with mirrors.
On some lasers, calibrating these mirrors can be a chore. Bambu Lab developed a laser alignment sensor, which clips to the toolhead and allows the laser to align the mirrors itself in just about a minute.
The Bambu Lab R1 has an excellent positioning system. There is a bird's eye camera on the lid of the laser, which requires that the lid be up when measuring. This takes a little getting used to since I reflexively shut the lid of a laser when I walk away from it. There is a camera mounted on the toolhead as well as a distance-measuring laser, instead of a clunky mechanical probe. The R1 tracks the toolhead position with XY encoders. The system worked great out of the box with no camera calibration needed. The camera is listed as having a .2mm positioning accuracy.
The Bambu Lab R1 is rated to cut up to 18mm wood and 20mm acrylic but doing so requires changing the focus lens in the tool head and then doing a five minute vision accuracy calibration. To change lenses, you need to remove two extremely tiny 1.5mm screws from the toolhead cover and four screws from the focus lens. It would be nice if they could develop a quick release for the lens, since as it is, this is not a process I’d want to have to do frequently.
A built-in air assist works to keep charring down and keep the laser lens clear. It is not adjustable, being either on or off, and it's powerful enough to move lightweight objects if they are not stuck down.
Given its size, the R1 is not likely to be used anywhere other than a shop or workroom, which is great because this thing is loud. The cooling fans in the laser don’t ever stop, and they are pretty loud on their own. When the laser is activated, it sounds like a jet engine spooling up. Between the noise of the laser and the air purification, it’s the loudest laser I’ve reviewed.
Assembling the Bambu Lab R1
The Bambu Lab R1 is fully assembled out of the box. Setup requires removing the accessory box, removing a cage around the tool head, and removing two stops holding the XY carriage in place for shipping. At initial power up the printer walks you through these steps from the touch screen.
There is a short calibration routine that automatically calibrates the laser’s mirrors by clipping the laser alignment sensor to the toolhead. In no time at all, you are ready to go.
The riser base comes in four large assemblies that are screwed together. You need to remove the base plate from the laser before setting it atop the riser. A data cable runs from the laser to the riser base, and requires deft hands to attach. Rubber feet on the bottom of the main laser unit hold it the correct position
The laser is cooled with a mixture of distilled water and antifreeze, which is poured into the rear of the laser with an included funnel. Pay close attention to the instruction booklet when adding coolant. The instructions call for “preparing” 1500ml of distilled water, then adding antifreeze to an indicated level on the rear sight window. But what it means is to pour in the antifreeze, then add as much of the 1500ml of water as needed to hit the correct level. Getting this backward makes a bit of a mess. After mopping up, I added the correct amount of water and coolant to the laser. The coolant must be topped off after turning the laser on, so don’t move the laser into a position where you cannot access the coolant port until you do this.
Safety Precautions for the Bambu Lab R1
The Bambu Lab R1 is a fully enclosed and safe Class 1 laser by itself. When running with the riser base and conveyor, it moves to a Class 4 laser. Operating a Class 4 laser requires laser-safe glasses that are not provided with the laser. I was not able to see any leakage of laser light through the riser base, but it is unavoidable when running with the conveyor. Laser light can cause severe damage to eyes and skin, and care should be taken to keep small children and pets away while the laser is in use.
The R1 has a number of built-in safety features. There is an equipment key preinstalled on the left side of the laser. When not in use this key can be pulled to prevent unauthorized access. The laser will not operate with the enclosure’s lid up and will quickly pause the job if the lid is raised while in use. If there is a problem with the job, the machine can be stopped from the touch screen, and for major problems, there is a red kill switch on the right side of the machine, which will quickly cut power to the machine completely. The laser has flame sensors which will stop the job if they detect any issues. Bambu Lab provided its optional auto fire-extinguishing system for the review. This unit has a replaceable gas canister and plugs into the left side of the laser.
Even with a good air purifier, some materials should not be burned with a laser due to their chemical makeup. Dallas Maker Space has published a list of safe and hazardous materials to use with their laser. The list of no-nos includes some plastics like PVC, fiberglass, and certain types of foams.
Software for the Bambu Lab R1
Bambu Suite was developed to run the lasers on the H series and also handle the cutting function on H2 and A2 printers. It might be the easiest to use laser software I’ve seen. The laser is connected to Wi-Fi from the touchscreen, and Bambu Suite connects to it just like a 3D printer. You import whatever you want to cut or engrave, choose the process type, hit Prepare, then select Measure, line up your art with the material, and pick the material you are using. Finally, you press Make and off it goes.
The only thing that the software doesn’t have is a large list of default materials. The basics are there, but hopefully more will be added over time. As it is, a number of the projects I did required internet searches and guesswork to find material settings that worked.
Makerworld is accessible directly from Bambu Suite, and it has an expanding group of shared laser projects to help you get started.
Engraving / Cutting with the Bambu Lab R1
For the first job, we used the test file from Bambu Lab that includes line drawing, engraving, and cutting on 3 mm basswood plywood. The test file did not list the settings, but the overall job took under two minutes to complete and looks really good. The cuts show much less charring than you would see on a diode laser.
Next, I tried a really intricate butterfly decoration from PabloLab on Makerworld.com. Using the default material settings for 3mm basswood, 75% power at 30 mm/s, the cut was perfect. The butterfly and the interior cuts dropped out of the material with no weeding needed. I should point out I broke off one of her antennae in handling.
The Bambu Lab R1 is rated to cut up to 18mm black walnut and 20mm acrylic, but the thicker wood requires the optional medium or long focus lenses. I tested cutting on a piece of pine lumber that is 19.5mm thick but is much softer than black walnut. There was no material default for anything thicker than 3mm. The cut on the left used the long focus lens and did the best cut at the lowest power, using 80% power at 10mm/s and 4 passes. The cut in the middle used the medium focus lens at 85% power at 5 mm/s and required 5 passes. The short focus lens really did not totally punch through the bottom of the material. The cuts are charred due to using 100% power at 4 mm/s through multiple tries.
For cutting out stickers out of sheets of sticker paper, we used the material preset for 200g kraft paper, 45% power at 250mm/s. The cuts were perfect and only took a few seconds. With a jig mounted on the cutting plate, the results are repeatable page after page.
There was no material preset for PETG so with a little trial and error we stepped that down to 65% power at 35mm/s for 2mm PETG and 20% power at 20mm/s for 1mm PETG. With air assist, the results were terrific, with just a very little smoke cloudiness at the edges of the PETG cuts. At these speeds, the cuts all took less than a minute.
Where most lasers just pass right through clear materials, CO2 lasers run at a high enough frequency to cut and engrave them. Using the shape library in Bambu Suite for the designs, we cut a bunch of blanks for use with our UV printer out of clear PETG sheets and clear acrylic. The material settings in Bambu Suite were perfect for 3mm clear acrylic at 80% power at 10mm/s speed.
CO2 lasers can also engrave glass with no masking needed, though a thin smear of liquid soap is suggested to keep chipping down. There was no material preset for glass, so a quick internet search led to settings from a competitor’s 55-watt CO2 laser. Using 30% power and 250mm/s, with air assist on, the engraving took just seconds and looks excellent.
CO2 lasers can’t cut metal, but they do a good job engraving coated metal. The Bambu lab R1has a curved surface machining mode for curved surfaces like this flask and tumblers. The auto measure function creates a 3D map of the material’s surface and shows the engravable area. Using the settings for aluminum business cards, 70% power at 400mm/s, the job took less than a minute and looks sharp and clear.
Bottom Line
The Bambu Lab R1 is an impressive step into the laser market. Good hardware with even better software makes the R1 an excellent choice for makers and small businesses needing an easy-to-use CO2 laser. It’s simple enough for a beginner to use, leaving you with more time to focus on making art, not fussing over settings.
Retailing at $2,499, the R1 is more expensive than a hobby-level diode, but a downright bargain compared to the competition. If you’re serious about making cool things or running a small business, the price is worth it.
By combining a 55W CO2, a generous 600 x 300 mm work area, and automated mirror calibration, it delivers high-grade cutting performance through wood, acrylic, and glass with minimal charring. While the manual lens swap process is a minor hassle and the operational noise requires a dedicated workspace or shop environment, its performance outclasses most competitors in its price range.
If you’re not ready to invest in a professional-grade machine, check out the Creality Falcon A1 Pro, a very capable 20W for $1,099. If you’re thinking about engraving glass or handling materials without charring, the xTool F2 Ultra UV is a great “cold” laser that runs for $4,299. If you want to take your laser with you, a portable xTool F1 laser is a heck of a deal at $819.
Denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

articles.title: Stanford-Tool verwandelt wissenschaftliche Papers in interaktive KI-Agenten
articles.text:
Studie als KI-Agent: Stanford-Tool macht Forschungsartikel interaktiv
Künstliche Intelligenz revolutioniert nicht nur die Forschung, sondern auch die Art und Weise, wie wissenschaftliche Studien geschrieben und veröffentlicht werden. Zuletzt drehte sich die Debatte darum, wie große Sprachmodelle genutzt werden können, um Studien zu bewerten. Eine neue Arbeit der Stanford University bringt nun KI-Agenten ins Spiel – mit dem Ziel, Forschungsergebnisse besser verständlich zu machen.
Durch KI-Agenten werden wissenschaftliche Paper interaktiv
Paper2Agent heißt das System, das ein Team rund um James Zou von der Stanford University School of Medicine entwickelt und kürzlich im Fachmagazin Nature veröffentlicht hat. Es verwandelt wissenschaftliche Manuskripte in interaktive KI-Agenten, die Fragen zur Arbeit beantworten, Ergebnisse validieren und sogar mit anderen Agenten kommunizieren können.
„Das ist eine Gelegenheit, das Wesen von Wissen grundlegend neu zu definieren“, sagt Studienleiter Zou. Bislang seien wissenschaftliche Arbeiten statische Aufzeichnungen in Form von gedruckten oder digitalen Texten. In Zeiten von agentischer künstlicher Intelligenz ändere sich das: Ein Framework wie Paper2Agent könne aus jeder statischen Arbeit eine interaktive machen. Man könne sich das wie einen „virtuellen Autor vorstellen, der weiß, wie Wissen entsteht“, sagt Zou.
Das Tool Paper2Agent ist auf Github frei verfügbar
Was dazu benötigt wird, ist eine wissenschaftliche Studie und der Paper2Agent Code, den die Forschenden kostenlos auf Github bereitstellen. Verknüpft man diesen mit einem Coding-Assistenten wie Claude Code, ist Paper2Agent in der Lage, die Arbeit in einen Model Context Protocol Server (MCP) zu übersetzen. MCP ist eine noch recht junge, offene Schnittstelle, mit der KI-Agenten mit anderen Systemen kommunizieren können. „Ein MCP ermöglicht es der KI im Grunde genommen, ein PDF-Dokument in einer Form darzustellen, auf die Agenten leicht zugreifen können – fast wie bei einem Ablagesystem“, sagt Zou.
Paper2Agent extrahiert vereinfacht gesagt das in der Arbeit enthaltene Wissen, den Studienaufbau und die Ergebnisse und setzt mit einem eigenen Multi-Agenten-System einen MCP-Server auf. Wird dieser dann mit einem Sprachmodell verknüpft, ist der Agent einsatzbereit: Die Nutzerinnen und Nutzer können ihm Fragen in natürlicher Sprache stellen, ihn bitten, die Methoden aus der Studie auf neue Datensätze anzuwenden, oder mehrere Paper-Agenten miteinander interagieren lassen. Das Aufsetzen des Agenten dauert pro Studie weniger als eine Stunde und die Kosten für die genutzt Rechenleistung bei etwa 15 US-Dollar liegen, heißt es in der Studie.
Wie werden Halluzinationen ausgeschlossen?
Um Halluzinationen zu minimieren, gleicht jeder Paper-Agent in einer iterativen „Build-Test-Repair-Schleife“ immer wieder die Ergebnisse und Zahlen aus der zugrundeliegenden Studie ab und wird abschließend „gesperrt“. Die Forscherinnen und Forscher können aber noch manuell Informationen ergänzen, etwa zu gescheiterten Experimenten, die es häufig nicht in die finale Arbeit schaffen, die aber dennoch wichtige Aussagen enthalten können.
Das Team aus Stanford hat inzwischen mehr als 100 Paper-Agenten aus Arbeiten aus verschiedenen Fachbereichen erstellt. Darunter war die Studie von Deepminds AlphaGenome, einem KI-Modell, das voraussagen soll, wie einzelne Gene bestimmte Prozesse im Körper steuern. Die Forschenden haben dem Agenten anschließend Testfragen zu bestimmten Genen gestellt, die sowohl konkret mit der Studie zu tun hatten, aber auch komplexere wissenschaftliche Aufgabenstellungen, für die das System selbstständig planen musste. Die Antworten wurden mit anderen, spezialisierten Agenten verglichen.
Test von Paper2Agent anhand der Studie zu AlphaGenome
Das Ergebnis: Paper2Agent erreichte, je nach Fragestellung, eine Genauigkeit zwischen 82 und 100 Prozent und übertraf dabei die bestehenden Systeme. Auf die Frage nach einer Gensquenz, die auf hohe Cholesterinwerte hindeutet, hat das System ein anderes Gen identifiziert als in der ursprünglichen Studie von Deepmind – aber eines, das im Rahmen der Hypothese dennoch denkbar ist. Die Forschenden sehen das als Beweis dafür, dass Paper2Agent auch für neue Forschung genutzt werden könnte.
Und nicht nur das: Das dank MCP verschiedene Agenten miteinander kommunizieren können, erhofft sich das Team auch eine Art KI-zu-KI-Kollaboration, durch die sich das Wissen, das bislang als statischer Text vorlag, künftig zu einer sich immer weiterentwickelnden, lebendigen Ressource wird.
„Früher mussten sich zwei Forschungsgruppen, die zwei unterschiedliche Artikel veröffentlichten, irgendwie selbst finden“, sagt Studienleiter James Zou. Künftig könne es ein „Manuskript-Speed-Dating“ in großem Maßstab geben: Millionen von Paper-Agenten, die künftig Gemeinsamkeiten untereinander aufdecken und zusammenarbeiten, um neue Erkenntnisse zu gewinnen.

articles.title: Getting ahead: 5 ways to break stress before it breaks you
articles.text:
Getting ahead: 5 ways to break stress before it breaks you
Practical strategies for reducing workplace stress and burnout
Technology is constantly evolving, and with that comes increasing pressure on those working in the sector. It's no surprise, then, that technology ranks among the industries with the highest levels of work-related stress, contributing to around 550,000 working days lost over three years according to the Health and Safety Executive in 2024.
Stress rarely appears overnight. It builds over time through heavy workloads, unclear expectations, limited support and constantly shifting priorities. Too often, leaders only recognize the problem once an employee has reached burnout.
Assistant Professor of Leadership Education at the University of Florida and a practitioner of Kirton’s Adaption-Innovation (KAI) Theory.
Managing stress shouldn't be seen solely as an individual's responsibility. Leaders play a vital role in creating environments where people feel supported, can raise concerns early and have the tools they need to manage pressure before it becomes overwhelming.
By recognizing the warning signs and making a few practical changes, leaders can help prevent stress from escalating into burnout.
1. Understand how and why individuals respond differently
Two employees can face exactly the same challenge but respond in completely different ways. One useful way of understanding these differences is through Kirton's Adaption-Innovation (KAI) Theory. Developed by psychologist Dr Michael Kirton, the theory suggests people naturally approach change and problem-solving in different ways.
More adaptive individuals tend to prefer structure, established processes and incremental improvements, while more innovative individuals are often more comfortable with ambiguity, risk taking and finding entirely new solutions. Most people fall somewhere between the two.
Neither style is better than the other, but each can bring different sources of stress. More adaptive employees may struggle with unclear roles, changing priorities or a lack of structure, while more innovative employees can become frustrated by rigid processes or repetitive work.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Understanding how individuals prefer to work allows leaders to allocate work more effectively, helping employees perform at their best while reducing unnecessary pressure.
2. Create a culture of asking questions
Many employees struggle to admit when they need help. We are often taught this is a sign of weakness and an indicator of capability.
Creating a culture of trust changes that. When people feel comfortable raising concerns, asking questions or admitting they are struggling, problems can be addressed before they become unmanageable.
Leaders set the tone. Asking for feedback, acknowledging your own mistakes and responding positively when employees raise concerns all help create psychological safety within a team. An open culture also makes it much easier to recognize when someone is beginning to struggle.
Changes such as withdrawing from colleagues, becoming more irritable, missing deadlines or struggling to prioritize work are often viewed as performance issues, when they may actually be signs of mounting stress.
Regular conversations, rather than relying solely on formal performance reviews, give leaders the opportunity to identify these warning signs early. Simple adjustments, such as redistributing workloads, clarifying priorities or removing unnecessary obstacles, can prevent stress from developing into burnout.
3. Observe your team to identify stress early
Stress rarely appears suddenly. It can build gradually, making it difficult to recognize until it begins to affect an employee's wellbeing or performance.
While you may be aware that a particular task or deadline is likely to create pressure, it can be harder to spot when longer-term stress is beginning to affect your team. Changes in behaviour can be early warning signs. An employee may start to withdraw from colleagues, become more irritable or defensive, miss deadlines or struggle to prioritize their workload.
As leaders, we can be quick to interpret these changes as performance issues. However, they may be indicators that someone is experiencing stress and needs additional support.
Regular check-ins, rather than relying solely on formal performance reviews, give leaders an opportunity to understand what's happening and address problems early. By noticing these changes, leaders can redistribute workloads, adjust expectations or remove obstacles before stress develops into burnout.
4. Give your employees control
Many employees experience stress because they feel they have little control over their work. Those in the technology sector often face tight deadlines, changing priorities, and high expectations. While we cannot remove all these pressures, we can provide autonomy to employees to help them be more successful.
Greater autonomy doesn't mean removing direction altogether. Leaders still need to set realistic expectations and help teams distinguish between what's genuinely urgent and what can wait. As a leader, you need to help your employees set realistic goals. You can help employees recognize what is urgent and prioritize their tasks effectively.
Employees who provide input and contribute in this way feel more in control and experience a higher level of buy in to team goals.
5. Create a culture that prioritizes recovery
We often mistake short-term performance for sustainable outcomes. However, we require time to recover not just as a reward, but as consistent practice. Employees need to be encouraged to take time to recuperate.
As a leader, the tone you set is seen and mimicked. If you’re not taking regular breaks, working at all hours of the night, and pushing through exhaustion, your employees will feel they need to do the same. Consider your own habits and then promote celebrating breaks, disconnection outside of working hours, using leave time, and establishing work-life balance.
It is easy to say, “do as I say not as I do.” However, this culture starts with you. Taking time to recover yourself helps you avoid burnout and be a better leader overall. It will also lead to long-term sustained performance over short bursts of success.
Stress will always be a part of the workplace. The goal is not to remove stress, but to prevent burnout and sustain performance.
As a leader, the ability to help your employees reduce stress is a shared responsibility between the individual, yourself, and your team. By understanding how individuals solve problems, creating an environment of trust, observing stress early on, increasing employee autonomy, and promoting recovery time, your organization can retain talent and build a healthier and more productive workforce.

articles.title: Noble Carbon will show how it’s making EV charger installs painless at TechCrunch Disrupt | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Plenty of people want to buy electric vehicles, but not everyone is prepared to shell out for an upgrade to their home’s electrical service just to add an EV charger. The worry is reasonable. One study found that upgrading things like electrical panels (that box in the garage or basement that delivers power throughout a home) can more than double charger installation costs.
Rather than rip out the old panel, Noble Carbon has developed circuit breakers that can take the headache out of installing an EV charger, or a heat pump or an induction stove for that matter.
The Pittsfield, Massachusetts, startup is one of 200 startups in this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield, a pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco in October in which 20 finalists will present on the main stage.
Noble Carbon’s breakers can adjust how much electricity they deliver to an EV charger in real time, allowing the chargers to squeeze into otherwise at-capacity panels.
Electrical panels in people’s homes are typically designed to handle absolute peak usage, something that might happen only “a handful of hours per year,” Spencer Fields, Noble Carbon’s head of marketing, told TechCrunch.
For example, if someone is hosting family for a holiday, they might find themselves simultaneously using the water heater, air conditioning, oven, and several TVs, all while every light is on in the house. The rest of the time, the electrical panel has room to spare.
In that scenario, Noble Carbon’s smart breakers would turn down the power flowing to the devices they control, essentially guaranteeing that the entire house doesn’t draw more power than the panel can provide.
“In order to avoid a main panel upgrade, you really only need control on your three to six largest loads [the biggest power-drawing appliances],” Fields said.
Co-founder and CEO Jared Lebos was inspired to create the product after experiencing rolling blackouts in his home country of South Africa. He worked with Andrew Crane, the company’s co-founder and CTO, to turn it into reality.
The result is a breaker that fits into existing slots in a home’s electrical panel and, according to the company, takes less than five minutes to install. Some of the startup’s employees have been testing the breakers in their homes for more than a year, and the product is now undergoing evaluation for UL certification, a widely recognized electrical safety standard.
Noble Carbon currently is partnering with the utility Eversource to install its breakers in up to 200 multifamily units in Massachusetts.

articles.title: PhonePe secures in-principle approval for UAE operations
articles.text:
PhonePe secures in-principle approval for UAE operations
PhonePe also intends to explore opportunities to support 'Aani' and 'Jaywan', the UAE's domestic payment rails, by leveraging its full-stack technology platform, per a statement.
Digital payments platform PhonePe has secured in-principle approval from the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) to launch operations in the Emirates, marking a major step forward in its international expansion plans.
The regulatory clearance covers two key licenses: Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes (RPSCS) and Stored Value Facilities (SVF). With initial steps complete, PhonePe is now working toward final authorisation before launching commercial operations in the region.
“The UAE’s vision and regulatory environment make it an ideal setting for our international journey,” said Ritesh Pai, CEO and Executive Director, International Payments at PhonePe, per a statement. “By combining world-class technology with local partnerships, PhonePe intends to support the strong economic and trade corridors connecting the UAE, India, and global markets.”
According to the statement, PhonePe’s expansion into the UAE aligns with the country’s Financial Infrastructure Transformation (FIT) programme, targeting deep integration with local financial ecosystems.
Upon its final launch, the platform plans to integrate into the UAE’s domestic payment rails called Aani and Jaywan, leveraging its full-stack technology platform that currently serves over 700 million users and 50 million merchants in India.
Through NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), PhonePe already allows Indian travelers in the UAE to make instant QR payments at NEOPAY and Network International terminals.

articles.title: Des Apple Watch Series 12 et Ultra 4 flambant neuves redémarrent toutes seules, sans explication
articles.text:
Depuis leur lancement vendredi, plusieurs propriétaires d’Apple Watch Series 12 et Ultra 4 rapportent des redémarrages inopinés. Des journaux de diagnostic partagés par certains utilisateurs pointent vers un timeout du Neural Engine, sans que l’origine exacte du problème soit encore établie.
À peine sorties de leur boîte, les nouvelles montres connectées d’Apple font déjà l’objet de plusieurs signalements de dysfonctionnements. Sur les forums de MacRumors, mais aussi sur Reddit et les forums d’assistance Apple, des utilisateurs décrivent un scénario similaire : l’écran affiche soudainement le logo Apple, puis la montre redémarre, parfois en pleine utilisation, parfois alors qu’elle est simplement portée au poignet. Apple n’a pour l’instant pas reconnu officiellement ce problème.
Des logs convergents pointent vers le Neural Engine
Le point commun entre plusieurs de ces témoignages apparaît dans les journaux de diagnostic. Au moins quatre propriétaires ont partagé des fichiers de type « panic-full » présentant un scénario similaire : le Neural Engine semble rester bloqué pendant environ deux secondes, avant qu’un mécanisme de surveillance du firmware ne déclenche un arrêt et force le redémarrage de la montre.
Les situations précédant les redémarrages varient fortement selon les utilisateurs. Certains rapportent le problème après avoir utilisé Siri, modifié un cadran, ouvert Plans ou l’App Store, passé un appel ou enregistré une séance de sport. D’autres indiquent que leur Apple Watch a redémarré alors qu’elle était simplement au repos. Les signalements concernent aussi bien watchOS 27.0 que la mise à jour proposée lors de la configuration de la montre.
Le Neural Engine est un composant matériel d’Apple consacré notamment aux traitements d’intelligence artificielle et d’apprentissage automatique. Un « timeout » dans les journaux signifie toutefois qu’une opération n’a pas répondu dans le délai prévu : il ne permet pas, à lui seul, de déterminer si le problème vient du logiciel, du matériel ou d’une interaction entre les deux.
Certains utilisateurs ont par ailleurs tenté de réinitialiser complètement leur montre, sans constater de résolution durable. L’un d’eux rapporte même avoir fait remplacer son Apple Watch Series 12 en Apple Store, avant de rencontrer de nouveau le même type de redémarrage sur l’appareil de remplacement. Ce cas rend moins évidente l’hypothèse d’un problème propre à une seule unité défectueuse, mais ne permet pas de déterminer l’origine du bug.
Plusieurs dizaines de témoignages, mais aucune cause établie
Au moment de la publication de l’article de MacRumors, environ trente propriétaires avaient signalé des redémarrages dans le fil consacré au problème. Plusieurs autres témoignages ont depuis été repérés sur différents canaux. Ces signalements montrent que le phénomène ne se limite pas à un seul utilisateur, mais ils ne permettent pas encore d’en mesurer la fréquence parmi l’ensemble des propriétaires d’Apple Watch Series 12 et Ultra 4.
Plus troublant encore, certains utilisateurs d’iPhone 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max rapportent eux aussi des redémarrages qu’ils associent à des problèmes du Neural Engine. Ces témoignages restent toutefois distincts de ceux concernant l’Apple Watch et aucun élément indépendant ne permet pour l’instant d’établir qu'ils ont une origine commune.
Si un lien entre les deux phénomènes venait à être confirmé, le problème pourrait alors concerner une composante plus largement utilisée dans la nouvelle génération de puces Apple. À ce stade, il ne s’agit toutefois que d’une hypothèse. En attendant une explication officielle, mettre sa montre à jour reste le seul geste qui vaille : plusieurs témoignages le confirment, une simple réinitialisation, elle, ne suffit pas toujours à faire taire le logo Apple qui s’invite sans prévenir.

articles.title: AI data center boom hits growing resistance as $68 billion in US projects are blocked or delayed
articles.text:
A hot potato: Data center developers are facing stronger resistance as they try to add capacity for AI workloads across the United States. The pushback is delaying or blocking projects worth tens of billions of dollars and prompting states and local governments to scrutinize their power, water and land-use demands. As the AI buildout accelerates, community opposition is becoming a material obstacle to the industry's ability to add computing capacity at the pace it wants.
Local opposition blocked or delayed 45 data center projects valued at $68 billion during the second quarter, according to Data Center Watch, a research initiative from AI intelligence company 10a Labs. The affected projects accounted for more than half of the large-scale data center developments the group began tracking during the period.
The disputes are centered on the practical demands of AI infrastructure. New facilities require large amounts of electricity, water and land, and often need new transmission lines, substations or other utility upgrades. In some areas, residents are challenging individual projects. Elsewhere, local governments are considering moratoriums or new rules before developers submit permit applications.
Data Center Watch said it identified 843 groups opposing data center development in 49 states. Hawaii was the only state without a group on its list. The organization also said 30 statehouses introduced or adopted measures related to data center siting, electricity use or water consumption.
"New groups continue to emerge, opposition is appearing across a wide range of states and jurisdictions, and online petition signatures continue to grow," Miquel Vila, the group's lead analyst, told Bloomberg.
The second-quarter total was below the first quarter, when Data Center Watch counted 75 contested projects with an estimated value of about $130 billion. But the latest figures show that resistance is affecting a large share of proposed developments, not just a few high-profile projects.
For the technology industry, the issue is becoming a constraint on AI expansion. Companies including Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet are building more and more data centers to support training and inference workloads, which require significant amounts of electricity and cooling.
Developers have pursued several approaches to meet those needs, including larger grid connections, dedicated generation and on-site power systems. Those plans can create additional opposition, especially when they involve natural gas generation or major utility infrastructure.
Water use is another concern. Operators have promoted cooling systems designed to reduce consumption, including closed-loop designs. Critics, however, argue that even more efficient systems can place pressure on local supplies when deployed at the scale required for major AI campuses.
Opposition has also spread through online campaigns. One petition against a proposed Tennessee project drew more than 500,000 signatures on Change.org during the quarter, Data Center Watch said. The group said the petition represented more than one-third of all signatures collected on the platform during that period.
Data Center Watch is also seeing similar campaigns outside the United States. The group expanded its reporting this year to include opposition in Europe, Australia, South Africa and other regions. Those efforts focus on many of the same issues seen in the US, including project approvals, power demand and water use.
"As with many other trends, the US has generally been at the forefront, but the phenomenon is increasingly becoming global," Vila said. "We anticipate that this will just become more prominent as data center development expands across the globe."

articles.title: Queda tiempo para que un robot humanoide te planche la ropa en casa, pero ya están fabricando coches en Hyundai
articles.text:
Durante años, hablar de robots humanoides era hablar del Atlas de Boston Dynamics. La empresa representaba la cúspide de la evolución de estas máquinas, pero al igual que sus robots, han dado tantas volteretas pasando de ser una escisión del MIT a parte de Google, luego de Softbank y, ahora, de Hyundai, que parecían algo mareados. Sin embargo, y mientras la robótica humanoide china florecía, Boston Dynamics andaba preparando algo: poner a sus Atlas a currar.
Y acaban de inaugurar un laboratorio en los que entrenarán de cara a un futuro en las fábricas de coches de Hyundai.
RMAC. Dentro del plan de capacitación de robots de Boston Dynamics, el nuevo Centro de Aplicaciones Robóticas (o RMAC) a las afueras de la ciudad estadounidense de Savannah se erige como un paso clave. Es como un campus en el que los robots van a entrenar para poder trabajar en algo de provecho el día de mañana dentro de las fábricas de Hyundai Motor Group.
En este entorno, los robots entrenarán en un entorno real como es la preparación de la logística y la organización de piezas de automóviles dentro de la cadena de montaje. La idea es que, para 2030, Atlas empiece a montar componentes y, con el tiempo, los robots asumirán tareas más humanas, como aquellas que tengan que ver con trabajos de movimientos repetitivos y tareas como levantar peso.
De prácticas. De momento, se trata sólo de un entrenamiento en un entorno controlado en el que hay una combinación de robots con sistemas de aprendizaje por refuerzo y de operación a distancia humano mediante. La idea es ver cómo se desenvuelven en estos entornos en los que comparten espacio con humanos y donde deben manipular piezas que a veces son simples, pero otras veces cuentan con elementos estéticos que deben respetar y no dañar.
Zack Jackowski, director de producto y tecnología de Boston Dynamics, ha comentado que hay una diferencia importante entre este centro de investigación y los ensayos anteriores de Atlas. Anteriormente, el robot operaba en un entorno muy controlado y en fases acotadas en el tiempo. Simplemente se trataba de recopilar datos para hacer evolucionar el sistema. En el RMAC, sin embargo, la idea es que aprendan porque, a medio plazo, saldrán al mundo laboral junto a humanos y otros robots.
Plan a mayores. La idea del grupo es empezar a meter la directa para colarse en la conversación de los robots humanoides no tanto en tecnología, que llevan años en esa conversación, sino en cuanto a viabilidad comercial. Cuando Hyundai se hizo con el 100% de Boston Dynamics no lo hizo sólo por amor al arte y esperan empezar a encontrar clientes interesados en las capacidades de la máquina. Que quieren venderlos, vaya, y el mejor escaparate es empezar a prepararlos para que el trabajo en sus propias fábricas sea el mejor escaparate de cara a conseguir compradores.
Para ello, planean el despliegue de 25.000 unidades de Atlas en las plantas globales de Hyundai y Kia a lo largo de los próximos años, y ahí hay dos piezas esenciales. Por un lado, una nueva fábrica en Estados Unidos capaz de producir 30.000 robots anuales. Por otro, una ampliación del RMAC prevista para el próximo año que pueda albergar no sólo más robots, sino otros entornos de trabajo simulado. La idea de Hyundai es contactar con otros sectores como el aeroespacial, los semiconductores o la logística para que el Atlas aprenda más cosas y sea útil en otros campos.
Con un ojo en una Europa envejecida. De momento, ese plan es muy estadounidensecentrista, pero como ha comentado el Korea Herald, Hyundai tiene la intención de llevar el Atlas a la planta de Nosovice. Es ahí, en República Checa, donde la compañía tiene la única planta de producción en la Unión Europea y el motivo por el que están interesados en expandirse precisamente ahí es porque se está produciendo una reducción de la fuerza laboral europea debido al envejecimiento de la población.
Porque las pirámides están como están y, de hecho, no es la primera vez que los robots humanoides se cuelan en la conversación cuando hablamos de ejecutar trabajos para los que parece no haber reemplazo humano. Lo hemos visto en China y también en Japón, países cuya pirámide poblacional cada vez tiene peor pinta.
Parte de la guerra de robots. Hablábamos antes de la industria china y no es para menos. Se estima que el gigante asiático fabrica el 90% de los robots humanoides del mundo debido a que lleva 20 años acumulando talento alrededor de esta industria, pero también a que fabrican todos los componentes necesarios para dar vida a estas máquinas, por lo que si quieren cualquier cosa, sólo tienen que cruzar la calle para conseguirlo.
Los 30.000 Atlas de Boston Dynamics al año es extremadamente ambicioso y un hito para la robótica humanoide estadounidense, sobre todo en un contexto en el que hay empresas como UBTech que ya están abriendo plantas en las que producir 10.000 robots humanoides industriales al año... y son sólo una de las muchas empresas que están haciendo lo mismo.
El objetivo de unos y otros es hacer que los robots dejen de ser simples monos de feria para convertirse en algo útil en comercios, logística, fábricas (Xiaomi también está probando sus propios robots para fabricar sus coches) o, directamente, como robots de compañía, por muy siniestro y a ciencia ficción que suene eso.

articles.title: Glorious GMMK Eternal Review: Fits anywhere, sounds great
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The GMMK Eternal isn't the most exciting keyboard, but it sounds good and takes up very little space.
Pros
- +Compact size that's not overly cramped
- +Excellent sound-damping
- +$100
Cons
- -OEM profile keycaps
- -Generic-looking
- -ABS keycaps in OEM profile
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Something, something, going back to your roots. I guess that's what Glorious is doing (or, thinks it's doing) with the GMMK Eternal — its new wired mechanical gaming keyboard.
The GMMK Eternal is, at a glance, pretty basic: it's wired, it has regular mechanical (not magnetic) switches and a standard 1,000 Hz polling rate. It comes with bright backlighting, double-shot ABS keycaps, and some gamer-friendly features such as multiple onboard profiles and macro-recording via Glorious Core. It also has a hot-swappable PCB and three layers of sound-dampening material in the case — it's not supposed to be a revolution, but it is a pretty solid option if you're looking for something compact and relatively budget-friendly. The GMMK Eternal is available now in black, with GMMK's Fox MX linear switches, for $99.99.
Design and Construction of the GMMK Eternal
The GMMK Eternal is a wired mechanical gaming keyboard with a compact 96-percent layout — it has a full function row, arrow keys, and a 10-key numberpad, but everything is squashed together (and it ditches most of the navigation keys), so it takes up significantly less space than a full-size keyboard but has almost as many keys. It sports a fairly simple, minimalist overall design — edge-to-edge keys with virtually no bezel, black anodized aluminum top plate over a black ABS plastic bottom case, and no obvious branding on the top or sides.
The keyboard measures approximately 14.6 inches (372mm) wide by 4.8 inches (122mm) deep, and is 1.7 inches (44mm) thick at its thickest point (including the keycaps). That's significantly smaller than a full-size keyboard, and is even small by 96-percent keyboard standards — perhaps my favorite 96-percent keyboard, the Asus ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless, is slightly larger than the GMMK Eternal at 14.84 x 5.16 inches (377 x 131mm), though at 1.57 inches (40mm) thick, it's slightly lower-profile. This is because the GMMK Eternal has double-shot ABS keycaps with shine-through legends in an OEM profile (the ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless comes with keycaps in a mid-height profile that's very close to the Cherry profile).
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
While the GMMK Eternal is pretty compact, even by 96-percent keyboard standards, you won't feel too cramped for space. There's enough room to leave some separation between the alphanumeric keys and the arrow keys (though not much), and there's enough room in the top row that the Function keys are grouped into visibly distinct groups of four. There are five navigation keys next to the Function row and above the numberpad: PrintScreen, Delete, Insert, Page Up, and Page Down. So you really shouldn't miss too much about your full-size board once you get used to the numberpad being right on top of you.
The GMMK Eternal has some weight to it, but it's not too hefty: it weighs in at just under two pounds (1.94 lbs / 879 g), which is about what we'd expect for a board of this size and construction. For comparison, the wired Corsair Vanguard Pro 96 weighs about 2.2 pounds (998g), while the wireless Asus ROG Strix Morph 96 Wireless weighs just under 2.5 pounds (2.48 lbs / 1,125 g). The GMMK Eternal is heavy enough that it shouldn't move around on your desk too much during heavy gaming sessions, but it's not so heavy that it would be difficult to travel with.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The bottom of the keyboard is where you'll finally see Glorious' branding. The Glorious name is stamped across the back, debossed with a shiny finish. There are also a couple strips of anti-slip rubber, as well as two sets of plastic flip-out feet for adjusting the keyboard's angle. The GMMK Eternal is a wired keyboard, and it has one USB-C port in the center of the board.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The GMMK Eternal comes with just two accessories in the box: a 6-foot (1.8m) rubber-coated USB-C to USB-A cable and a 2-in-1 combination keycap and switch puller.
Specs
| Size | 96% | 
| Number of keys | 99 | 
| Switches | Glorious Fox Switches | 
| Backlighting | Yes | 
| Onboard Storage | Yes (3 profiles) | 
| Dedicated Media Keys | No | 
| Game Mode | Yes / No | 
| Additional Ports | 0 | 
| Connectivity | Wired (USB-C) | 
| Cable | 6ft. / 1.8m USB-C to USB-A | 
| Keycaps | double-shot ABS | 
| Construction | Anodized aluminum top plate ABS bottom case | 
| Software | Glorious Core | 
| Dimensions (LxWxH) | 14.6 x 4.8 x 1.7" / 372 x 122 x 44mm | 
| Weight | 1.94lbs / 879g | 
| MSRP / Price at Time of Review | $99.99 | 
| Release Date | Sept. 8, 2026 | 
Typing and Gaming Experience on the GMMK Eternal
The GMMK Eternal is a mechanical gaming keyboard with a hot-swappable PCB that takes both 3- and 5-pin switches. It comes pre-built with Glorious' Fox switches, which are pre-lubed linear switches with an actuation force of 55g — a little heavier than your average linear switch, but I kind of liked the extra force. The switches are otherwise typical linear switches, with smooth, stable keypresses that have no tactile bump or audible click. They're rated for 50 million clicks.
The keyboard features three layers of sound-dampening material in the case: a molded silicone layer and two layers of PU foam around the PCB, for a "deeper, more satisfying thock." And I'll admit that I was pretty impressed with how the GMMK Eternal sounded out of the box — especially for a sub-$100 keyboard from a mainstream gaming company. There was a small amount of rattle as I typed, but the case, at least, was solid and ping-less, and bottoming out did give a deeper sound (if not quite a "thock").
The GMMK Eternal comes with double-shot ABS keycaps in an OEM profile, which is the standard, medium-height profile you'll find on most mainstream gaming keyboards. The keycaps have lightly cupped, textured tops with shine-through legends and secondary legends printed on the sides in white. While I usually prefer lower-profile keycaps, I didn't mind these — the keyboard is fairly compact and low-profile to begin with, so I didn't find the standard height OEM profile to be uncomfortable (nor did I feel like I needed a wrist rest).
The GMMK Eternal is a solid option for both typing and gaming — I didn't have any issues with accuracy, speed, or response time in my testing, minus the normal learning curve of getting used to having the arrow keys right on top of the alphanumeric keys.
Features and Software of the GMMK Eternal
The GMMK Eternal is configurable with Glorious' universal peripheral software, Glorious Core, which I don't have any real problems with, save for the fact that it requires a restart upon install. The keyboard has onboard storage, and you can set up up to three profiles in Glorious Core to save directly to the hardware.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You can use Glorious Core to adjust the keyboard's settings, including polling rate, input latency, and lighting standby timer, as well as switching between Windows and Mac modes. This isn't a magnetic switch keyboard, so there's not much else to set up in terms of performance. You can also remap keys — up to two layers deep, and the software has a built-in macro recorder and manager.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You can also customize the keyboard's lighting, which looks great — the board features bright RGB backlighting with a north-facing PCB, and the board's otherwise boring design really lets the lighting shine. There are 17 different lighting presets in Glorious Core, and you can also customize the lighting for each key individually (if you want).
The Bottom Line
The Glorious GMMK Eternal isn't the most exciting keyboard on the market, especially not for gaming. It's a wired keyboard with mechanical switches and a standard 1,000 Hz polling rate, so it's not trying to be the fastest, lowest-latency, RapidTrigger-enabled keyboard that will launch you into a pro-eSports career. Instead, it's a simple, compact keyboard that offers a very solid typing and gaming experience with hot-swappable switches and pretty RGB lighting for the relatively budget-friendly price of $100. While you can definitely find keyboards for less than $100, you probably won't find one that sounds and feels better than the GMMK Eternal.
Sarah Jacobsson Purewal is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware covering peripherals, software, and custom builds. You can find more of her work in PCWorld, Macworld, TechHive, CNET, Gizmodo, Tom's Guide, PC Gamer, Men's Health, Men's Fitness, SHAPE, Cosmopolitan, and just about everywhere else.

articles.text:
Galaxy S25 Ultra com Snapdragon tem 58% OFF em oferta agressiva
Galaxy S25 Ultra (256 GB) com chip Snapdragon de ponta e câmera de 200 MP sai 58% mais barato que o preço original, em oferta do Magalu no Pix com cupom
O Galaxy S25 Ultra de 256 GB está em oferta por R$ 5.099 no Pix com cupom INFLU300 no Magazine Luiza. O celular premium da Samsung, com chip Snapdragon de ponta, tela AMOLED de 120 Hz e câmera principal de 200 MP, recebe desconto de 58% sobre o preço original de R$ 11.999.
O S25 Ultra entrega desempenho de ponta graças ao kit interno, que inclui o chip Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite e 12 GB de RAM, que sustentam apps pesados, games e soluções do Galaxy AI localmente. Os 256 GB de armazenamento disponibilizam espaço interno adequado para guardar vídeos e fotos.
Sua tela AMOLED Dinâmico 2X de 6,9″ possui taxa de 120 Hz e brilho de até 2.600 nits, combinação capaz de reproduzir imagens com cores vibrantes e alta fluidez nas transições em apps e games, além de ter visibilidade garantida em qualquer ambiente.
O kit principal de câmeras filma em 8K. Ele é formado por uma wide de 200 MP com OIS e uma ultrawide de 50 MP, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, uma telefoto de 10 MP com zoom óptico de 3x e uma periscópica de 50 MP e 5x para aproximações com qualidade. A frontal de 12 MP filma em 4K a 60 fps e tira ótimas selfies.
O corpo de titânio do S25 Ultra é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Gorilla Armor 2, resistente contra riscos e arranhões, enquanto a certificação IP68 confere proteção em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.000 mAh resiste a até 31 horas de reprodução de vídeo, segundo a Samsung. O suporte ao carregamento rápido de 45 W via USB-C e de 15 W sem fio permite o uso prolongado por um dia inteiro, recurso essencial para usuários com agendas corridas.
O Galaxy S25 Ultra de 256 GB (R$ 5.099 no Pix com cupom INFLU300) será atualizado até o Android 22 e conversa com redes 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.
