articles.title: NASA chief: I'm only interested in "good deals" from international partners
articles.text:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman speaks at AFA's Air, Space & Cyber Conference on September 15, 2025.
Credit:
Jud McCrehin/Air & Space Forces Association
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman speaks at AFA's Air, Space & Cyber Conference on September 15, 2025.
Credit:
Jud McCrehin/Air & Space Forces Association
NASA must be more selective in the way it forges international partnerships as the race to the Moon transforms from a battle for national prestige between the United States and China into a high-stakes competition for extraterrestrial real estate and resources, the agency’s administrator said.
Jared Isaacman, now in his 10th month at the helm of the world’s largest civilian space agency, told a gathering of military leaders and defense contractors last week near Washington, DC, that the 21st-century race to the Moon is more than a battle of ideologies. The sweet spot for a Moon base, Isaacman said, is a relatively small region near the lunar south pole, and there are tangible implications for who gets there first.
The Moon’s south pole harbors substantial quantities of water ice concentrated on the floors of craters away from the reach of sublimating rays of sunlight. The ice inside these eternally dark craters could be used to supply water, air, and rocket fuel for a Moon base, supporting a permanent settlement and providing a springboard for future expeditions to Mars.
“It’s a big Moon, with the surface area of Africa,” Isaacman said Wednesday at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference. “The south pole is more akin to Washington, DC, when there are only so many roads and so many good parking spots that you’re going to want to occupy.”
“We want to go there to master the skills for Mars,” Isaacman said. “And when you realize there are only limited parking spots that get us access to that training environment, it creates an urgency, and we must [go fast] because the Chinese are going to the exact same locations. They are partnered with the Russians. They are going to put a nuclear reactor there, and they could potentially deny this training environment that is a necessity for America’s space ambitions.”
Isaacman said this means NASA must make better decisions on when and how to work with international partners. Other nations have a place in NASA’s programs, but only if they can meaningfully contribute to the mission, he said.
“I will tell you, though, and this is right from the top from the president of the United States: We’re only doing good deals, and we haven’t always done good deals,” Isaacman said. “There was absolutely a time where we were trying [to] make everyone happy. Let’s get a lot of flags together for a great press release, and it can [be], and absolutely has been, at times, a drag on the mission instead of accelerating it. You can’t do that, and we’ve changed that now, and as a result, good deals are happening.”
The rim crest and upper part of the rim of Shackleton Crater, as viewed by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. The Moon’s south pole is located on the rim near the upper-right corner of the image.
Credit:
NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University
The rim crest and upper part of the rim of Shackleton Crater, as viewed by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. The Moon’s south pole is located on the rim near the upper-right corner of the image.
Credit:
NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University
What’s a good deal?
Isaacman singled out as a good deal NASA’s agreement with the Italian government in March for the development of living quarters for astronauts on the Moon.
“They’re committing over $5 billion to building one of the first habitation modules,” Isaacman said. “It likely will be the first real habitation module that makes its way to the lunar surface. And as a result, you’re going to see two Italian astronauts on the surface of the Moon.”
Japan, too, is coming in clutch for NASA, Isaacman said, with a multibillion-dollar commitment to develop a pressurized rover to ferry astronauts across the Moon. In exchange, Japan will likewise get two tickets to the Moon for the country’s astronauts. The US and Japanese governments signed the agreement on the pressurized rover in 2024.
“That is the expectation we set for everyone,” Isaacman said. “You’re not just going to bring us a list and say, ‘I will do this regardless if it helps the mission or competes with US industry and what US industry is trying to accomplish on the Moon.’ That is not going to work. We need meaningful contributions now. The game has changed.”
The role of the European Space Agency, perhaps NASA’s most enduring international partner, on the Moon Base program remains undefined. ESA signed up to provide elements for a habitation module, a refueling module, and deep space communications hardware for the planned Gateway mini-space station in orbit around the Moon.
Canada, too, is weighing its potential contribution to the Moon Base program. The Canadian Space Agency was on the hook to build a robotic arm for the Gateway outpost, improving on the Canadian robotics systems used on the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station. The design and use case for a robotic arm on the surface of the Moon, where it must operate in partial gravity, is different from that in microgravity. It doesn’t help that the Trump administration is currently engaged in a trade war with Canada, erecting a hurdle for any potential bilateral agreements.
ESA and Canada received guarantees from NASA for lunar flight opportunities for their astronauts through their agreements on Gateway. ESA also provides service modules for NASA’s Orion spacecraft, the ship that carries astronauts between the Earth and the Moon. Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen took Canada’s first seat on an Artemis mission with the flight of Artemis II around the Moon earlier this year.
NASA announced in June that ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano, a colonel in the Italian Air Force, will serve as pilot on the Artemis III mission to test lunar landers and the Orion spacecraft in low-Earth orbit in 2027.
Rule by committee
ESA’s director general, Josef Aschbacher, told reporters in June that he is eager to secure seats for the agency’s astronaut corps to land on the Moon. A “meaningful” contribution to the Moon Base program would pay the fare, but it hasn’t been easy to find agreement on what that might look like.
NASA’s agreement with Italy, an ESA member state, was directly negotiated between the two countries outside the halls of ESA. The European Space Agency has 23 member states, which provide funding in three-year increments, offering a modicum of stability for ESA’s programs at the expense of agility.
Italy’s commitment to build a habitation module and Japan’s contribution of a pressurized rover offer something new to NASA, which didn’t have contracts with US companies to do that work. Those are the kinds of partnerships Isaacman said he is looking for.
ESA’s Argonaut would include elements from across Europe.
Credit:
European Space Agency
ESA’s Argonaut would include elements from across Europe.
Credit:
European Space Agency
“We had one partner that said, ‘Look, I’ll give you a lander, a robotic lander, that’ll go to Shackleton Crater by the mid-2030s,” Isaacman said in a question-and-answer session at the Air, Space & Cyber Conference last week. “I was like, ‘The Chinese are launching there in two months (with Chang’e 7, a mission now delayed to early 2027). What good is that to us then? There will be no landing spots available at that point in time.'”
Isaacman did not identify which partner he was talking about, but it almost certainly was ESA, which is seeking a role for its Argonaut cargo lander in NASA’s Moon Base program. The problem from NASA’s perspective is that Argonaut would replicate much of what US companies are well along in developing.
Each Argonaut lander could deliver to the lunar surface up to 1.5 metric tons (3,300 pounds) of cargo, such as crew provisions, science instruments, and infrastructure, according to ESA. That is half of the payload capacity of Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 1 lander, set to make its first flight to the Shackleton Connecting Ridge near the Moon’s south pole next year and far below the cargo capability of larger human-rated landers like Blue Moon Mark 2 or SpaceX’s Starship.
“We’ve got to get in touch with reality and make meaningful contributions to what NASA and the free world are trying to achieve with our space ambitions,” Isaacman said.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: Silent Hill: Townfall starts incredibly strong but gets maddeningly tedious
articles.text:
Scotland is a place that’s near and dear to my heart. Because my maternal grandparents hail from the country, I’ve travelled there several times and the culture as a whole has been a part of my life here in Canada. While I unfortunately haven’t returned in many years, Silent Hill: Townfall made me feel like I’ve been transported there.
It’s hard to explain. There’s something uniquely special about the country, like a pervasive warm coziness that seeps through its old architecture and rural towns, and Glaswegian developer Screen Burn so vividly captures all of that in Townfall while twisting it on its head. Set in 1996 in the fictional coastal village of St. Amelia (based on the real St. Monans), Townfall follows an American named Simon Ordell (The Leftovers‘ Jovan Adepo) as he washes ashore with no memory, IVs attached to him, and visions of a nurse named Zoe.
Admittedly, the premise of a man pursuing a woman in a mysterious fog-filled town is very similar to the likes of Silent Hill 2, but developer Screen Burn moves beyond the familiar trauma metaphors to explore corporate malfeasance and Thatcherism, particularly with respect to its impact on the healthcare system. The town also gets drenched in an eerie, almost apocalyptic shade of red, which introduces strange metallic pipes that block previously accessible routes and even hint at cosmic horror elements. All of this gives Townfall a unique flavour within the Silent Hill pantheon, even as Simon himself can often be a decidedly muted character.
And the first few hours of the game are truly sublime. Through the series’ first-ever full first-person POV, all of St. Amelia’s little corner shops, pharmaceutical ads and charity boxes feel all the more tactile and lived-in. The sense of haunting atmosphere is palpable here; gone are the typically friendly Scots who would populate these places, a feeling of isolation that’s only enhanced by eerie lighting in the streets and Canadian Pilotpriest’s moody ambient score.
The only others here, naturally, are monsters, represented here in the form of Slender Man-esque creatures that shamble and wail along the streets. And in a refreshing change of pace from last year’s ridiculously action-focused Silent Hill f, Townfall emphasizes stealth, so your best course is to try to steer clear of these fiends. While Simon can use a small assortment of weapons that include wooden planks, steel pipes and a revolver, combat is deliberately sluggish and durability and ammo are markedly minimal to make each encounter feel harrowing.
Instead, you have to use a handheld CRTV to track the ever-changing locations of enemies and attempt to skirt around them with the help of throwable objects and other sources of noises to distract them. This creates a nail-biting sense of tension as you hear a radio crackle to denote a nearby enemy, especially when there are multiple in the vicinity, and you can only monitor one at a time. Sometimes, I’d find myself trying to crouch-walk away from one, only to be discovered by another, frantically running into a nearby convenience store and locking the door for momentary respite. Other instances make smart use of the 90s setting, like an apartment in which I had to print photos in an adjacent room using a slow dial-up computer while an enemy was nearby. Sequences where you don’t have access to the CRTV, naturally, are all the more distressing.
Unfortunately, Townfall ruins this incredibly measured sense of tone and pacing by later throwing in a new recurring enemy type known as The Weight. This hulking brute is practically invincible, can run extremely fast and kills you in one shot, making him feel painfully unfair. What’s more, he’s first introduced in a basement setting in which you have to methodically check one of many rooms for the necessary items to progress, which becomes tedious as he’s constantly hounding you and, sometimes, even blocks your path.
And because these areas are comparatively much more claustrophobic and dimly lit than the streets of St. Amelia, it’s not like you can even easily sneak around him. It often just felt like trial and error of attempting to search one room, dying to him, then repeating with subsequent rooms. This sense of frustration is compounded by the fact that The Weight actively counters the IV drip system, which lets you combine materials to revive yourself upon death. Sometimes, I’d come back to life, only for The Weight to suddenly circle back and kill me again.
If I’m being generous, it would seem like this was an attempt at a stalker-type enemy like Mr. X from Resident Evil, but The Weight is far too nimble, erratic and powerful to evoke the same kind of looming threat. Instead, it’s just overbearing and completely upends the compelling gameplay loop.
Ultimately, Silent Hill: Townfall is worth playing due to its immaculate sense of place and (often) tightly-crafted fear-inducing stealth sequences. Just know that there’s more than a wee bit of a tedious grind in between those highs.
Silent Hill: Townfall launches on PS5 and PC on Sept. 24.

articles.title: Wie bei kostenlosen Handyspielen: Xbox könnte bald Werbepausen einblenden
articles.text:
Wie bei kostenlosen Handyspielen: Xbox könnte bald Werbepausen einblenden
Microsoft hat ein neues Patent für die Einblendung von Werbung in Spielen angemeldet. Die Technologie nutzt eine strenge Filterlogik: Eine Werbepause soll nur dann ausgelöst werden, wenn die Nutzer:innen sich gerade nicht in einer intensiven Szene befinden. Dadurch soll der Spielfluss möglichst wenig unterbrochen werden.
Werbung wird als störend empfunden
Die Gaming-Industrie ist riesig und wird oft unterschätzt. Tatsächlich spielen 55 Prozent der Deutschen zumindest ab und zu Video- oder Computerspiele, was rund 39 Millionen Menschen entspricht. Vor allem bei den Jüngeren ist der Anteil hoch: So gaben 89 Prozent der 16- bis 29-Jährigen an, gelegentlich zu zocken. Bei den über 65-Jährigen sagte das immerhin fast jede:r Vierte. Bei vielen haben Games einen festen Platz im Leben. Fast die Hälfte kann sich ein Leben ohne Video- und Computerspiele inzwischen nicht mehr vorstellen, und 44 Prozent haben sich schon einmal gewünscht, selbst in ein Spiel eintauchen zu können. Mehr als jede fünfte Person sagt sogar, dass sie nur in Spielen ihr wahres Ich zeigt.
Gamer:innen investieren nicht nur Zeit, sondern auch Geld in ihr Hobby. Drei Viertel von ihnen haben in den vergangenen zwölf Monaten Geld für Video- oder Computerspiele ausgegeben, die meisten davon online. Jeweils 48 Prozent tätigten In-Game-Käufe oder bezahlten für Abonnements. Zusätzliche Kaufangebote sorgen allerdings für Kritik: 58 Prozent stören sich daran und ein Drittel fühlt sich bei In-Game-Käufen häufig abgezockt. Gleichzeitig lehnen viele solche Modelle nicht grundsätzlich ab: 43 Prozent spielen lieber kostenlos mit In-Game-Käufen als kostenpflichtig ohne weitere Kosten. Das hat eine repräsentative Bitkom-Befragung unter 1.205 Personen in Deutschland ab 16 Jahren ergeben.
So könnte das neue Werbeformat für Games funktionieren
Künftig könnten Gamer:innen in PC- und Xbox-Spielen noch mehr Werbeeinblendungen sehen. Microsoft hat in den USA ein Patent für eine Werbeform eingereicht, die als „kontextbezogen” beschrieben wird und sich an bestimmten „Auslöse-Ereignissen” orientiert. Das „Ad-Credit“-System weist Spieler:innen Zeitblöcke ohne Werbung zu. Läuft ein Block ab, zeigt das Spiel beworbene Inhalte an und unterbricht dabei den Ablauf – ähnlich wie bei vielen kostenlosen Handyspielen. Anzeigen erscheinen in Abschnitten, die das System als Pausen erkennt. Die patentierte Technologie soll dabei erfassen, was im Spiel geschieht, sodass sie den Ablauf theoretisch nicht stört. Als mögliche Beispiele nennt das Patent Ladebildschirme und den Moment nach Abschluss einer Mission.
Das Patent mit dem Titel „Kontextbezogene Zugriffssteuerung für interaktive Anwendungssoftware” zielt darauf ab, die Monetarisierungslücke zwischen Free-to-Play-Spielen und kostenpflichtigen Games zu schließen, indem Werbung nur an natürlichen Unterbrechungspunkten erscheint. Gerüchten zufolge arbeitet Microsoft daran, den Game-Pass seiner Xbox-Konsole erneut umzugestalten, um einen günstigere, werbefinanzierten Tarif einzuführen. Laut Eurogamer hat Microsoft das Gerücht nicht direkt dementiert, sondern erklärt, man „teste regelmäßig verschiedene Game-Pass-Angebote und prüfe, was für Spieler:innen in verschiedenen Märkten am besten funktioniert”. Auch Windows Central hat darüber berichtet. Demzufolge könnte die Umstrukturierung im kommenden Jahr bekannt gegeben werden.

articles.title: ‘We’ll be the first to mine Bitcoin in space’ says Nvidia-backed startup —Starcloud will fire up its ASICs after its second spacecraft reaches orbit later this year
articles.text:
‘We’ll be the first to mine Bitcoin in space’ says Nvidia-backed startup —Starcloud will fire up its ASICs after its second spacecraft reaches orbit later this year
Almost constant solar energy plus ASIC price per KW are the most compelling aspects of the plan.
An Nvidia-backed startup plans to establish a Bitcoin mining operation in space before the year is out. Starcloud will fire up its cryptocurrency mining ASICs after its second spacecraft reaches orbit later this year. “We’ll be the first to mine Bitcoin in space,” claimed Starcloud CEO Philip Johnston in a recent interview with Documenting Bitcoin.
Starcloud was founded in 2024 with the headlining goal of moving data centers to space. “As launch costs fall, data centers in space will leverage continuous solar energy and radiative cooling, rapidly scaling to gigawatts while avoiding permitting constraints on Earth,” reads its mission statement. The firm spells out its proposition in far greater detail in a white paper on its website, highlighting the appeal of training AI in space. However, the ample supply of solar energy is also great for cryptomining.
So, when Starcloud-2 reaches orbit, it will be tasked with raising some crypto-cash. In the embedded interview segment, Johnston said: “We’ll have some Bitcoin mining ASICs on the second spacecraft launching later this year.” At the time of writing 1BTC is worth roughly $86,000, quite a way down from highs several months ago.
Starcloud-2 is just the second of four currently planned satellite launches from the startup. It is framed as the company's first commercial mission, and like the prior satellite, will feature a GPU cluster. Interestingly, the official Starcloud-2 project page doesn’t mention Bitcoin mining or ASICs, so Johnston’s reveal is quite eyebrow-raising. Moreover, for something that seems a bit like an afterthought, “Potentially it [Bitcoin mining] is one of the most compelling use cases of space compute,” the Starcloud CEO told Documenting Bitcoin.
Johnson provided some financial insight into why there is now a Bitcoin side gig or pivot being considered. He cited the lower costs of ASICs vs. GPUs: they are about 30x cheaper than GPUs per kilowatt, he told the host. A specific example given was a 1KW Nvidia B200 chip at $30,000 vs. a 1KW ASIC at $1,000. Solving the energy supply situation in space for GPUs, or for ASICs, isn’t relevant to the business, said Johnson. We wonder what Nvidia will think about that.
While the availability of near-uninterrupted solar power is a big attraction of space-based compute, there are downsides. For example, satellites aren’t easy to service, and convection cooling doesn’t work in a vacuum. Commercial space-based data centers are so new that some of the problems and solutions will only become entirely clear after pioneering deployments like the Starcloud-2.

articles.title: Meta gives Prospect Union access to UK employees ahead of new deadline
articles.text:
Meta is finally letting its UK staff join a union — and it could spark a national surge in union membership
Prospect union has been given access to UK employees
- Meta reaches agreement to allow Prospect union access to UK employees
- New reforms under the Employment Rights Act 2025 come into force in October 2026
- Despite slipping steadily, UK union membership could see a major bounce back
Meta has reached an agreement with Prospect union to allow access to its UK employees to speak about membership opportunities.
The move comes as a deadline for compliance with new union membership rules under the Employment Rights Act 2025 looms in October 2026.
Under the agreement, Prospect will have access to all 5,000 of Meta’s UK employees, allowing the union to talk to Meta workers about the benefits of union membership and recruit workers.
New union rules strengthen UK workers
A spokesperson for Meta said, “Employees who want to find out more about union membership have a straightforward way to do so. Meta's industrial relations team already works with employee representative groups in multiple markets, and we are approaching this in the same way.”
Initial trade union reforms as part of the Employment Rights Act 2025 took effect in February of this year. But subsequent reforms, due to take effect on 30 October, add additional requirements for employers to inform workers of their right to join a union, provide greater access for unions to workplaces, add additional protections for union representatives, and give workers greater protections when taking industrial action.
Meta is therefore providing Prospect with access to Meta employees ahead of the deadline, which Mike Clancy, General Secretary of Prospect, said “is to Meta’s credit that they have struck this voluntary deal with Prospect, rather than waiting for the new Right of Access to kick in, sending a positive message to staff that they are open to engaging with a union.”
Prospect currently has over 160,000 UK workers within its membership pool, covering technology, broadcasting, creative industries, defense and education.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The beginnings of a UK union bounce back?
According to official statistics from the UK Department for Business & Trade, union membership has been on a steady decline. In 1995, 28.8% of those in employment belonged to a union. But by 2025, this number has reached a historic low of just 19.9%.
Ahead of the reforms introduced by the Employment Rights Bill, union membership as a percentage of those in employment rose to 20.4% in 2025, potentially being bolstered ahead of the Bill’s formal introduction.
There are a number of reasons for the steady decline in union membership - some good, and some bad. The UK economy shifting away from industrial industries that traditionally held union-heavy employment is one of the most significant factors.
But Anti-union legislation introduced under Margaret Thatcher’s premiership during the 1990s also weakened the power of unions significantly. Unions lost legal protections against strikes, outlawed sympathy strikes, and introduced mandatory secret votes on union leadership ahead of strike action.
New rules introduced as part of employment protections and regulations - such as the minimum wage introduced in 1998 - have also reduced the need for unions to negotiate fair pay or organise industrial action in events of extreme unfairness.
Looking forward, the rapid introduction of AI to UK industries and the fear of job displacement are also likely fueling union membership in the UK.

articles.title: Freedom Mobile to shutter 3G in part of Ontario next month
articles.text:
Canada’s ongoing 3G shutdown is coming to a new region next month.
Starting Oct. 17, 2026, Freedom Mobile says it will start shutting down 3G in the Peterborough, Ont., region. This comes after Freedom shuttered 3G in the Ottawa-Gatineau region and across Quebec in July, and in Manitoba last year. Notably, SaskTel is also set to shutter its 3G network in October.
Most Canadian wireless providers aim to shutter 3G networks by March 2027. Bell, Telus, and Freedom all cite that date on their respective 3G shutdown support pages, while Rogers completed its 3G shutdown last year.
Carriers are shutting down 3G in order to enhance LTE and 5G networks, but the move is impacting Canadians using older devices or ones that aren’t officially supported by Canadian carriers.
The core issue relates to Voice over LTE (VoLTE) technology, which is used to transmit phone calls over LTE networks. However, phones that don’t support VoLTE, either because they’re too old or because they’re not compatible with Canadian carriers’ VoLTE systems, fall back to 3G networks to make phone calls. That means those devices will no longer be able to place phone calls once the 3G network is retired.
Most Canadian carriers offer tools on their websites for users to check if their device is compatible with VoLTE. So, if you’re not sure, that’s a great place to start. For some people, the solution will be as simple as turning on VoLTE in their device’s settings app. Others may have to upgrade to a newer phone.
Unfortunately, Canadians carriers typically only ensure compatibility with the smartphones they sell, which has left some people in a lurch. For example, many OnePlus devices that are capable of VoLTE were facing issues during Rogers’ 3G shutdown last year. OnePlus ultimately pushed an update to address the problem, but it’s worth keeping in mind that some phone brands may face compatibility issues if they’re not available from Canadian carriers.

articles.title: Plaque d’immatriculation verte en France : voici ce qu’elle signifie et comment la déchiffrer
articles.text:
Vous avez peut-être déjà aperçu sur les routes françaises des véhicules présentant une plaque d’immatriculation verte avec des caractères blancs. Mais que signifie-t-elle ? Bien loin d’être un simple détail esthétique, la couleur verte renseigne en réalité sur un statut particulier, qui peut donner droit à certains privilèges sur les routes. Aussi, comment lit-on ces plaques ? On vous explique tout.
Que signifient les plaques d’immatriculation vertes ?
Bien entendu, si ces plaques d’immatriculation sont vertes, ce n’est pas par souci d’esthétique. En réalité, elles indiquent un statut particulier. Une plaque verte signale ainsi qu’un véhicule est rattaché à une mission diplomatique, à un corps consulaire, à un chef de mission diplomatique ou encore à une organisation internationale.
Pour les forces de l’ordre, les plaques vertes n’impliquent en aucun cas une immunité sur les routes. Cependant, elles donnent une information sur le statut du véhicule et indiquent tout de même certains privilèges qui peuvent être accordés en fonction du statut de son titulaire. Cela peut notamment concerner certaines immunités liées aux fonctions diplomatiques ou consulaires. Mais comment identifier précisément ce statut ? Tout simplement en lisant la plaque d’immatriculation.
Comment lire ces plaques ?
Il existe plusieurs combinaisons de chiffres et de lettres pour les plaques d’immatriculation vertes, mais, par souci de clarté, nous allons ici nous baser sur l’une des plus répandues : le modèle 123 A 12345. Les premiers chiffres, avant la lettre, permettent d’identifier le pays ou l’organisation auquel le véhicule est rattaché. À titre d’exemple, le numéro 5 indique l’Allemagne, le numéro 115 la Russie et le numéro 401 l’UNESCO. Ensuite, nous retrouvons une à trois lettres qui renseignent sur le statut diplomatique du véhicule. Ainsi, « C » correspond au corps consulaire, « CD » au corps diplomatique et « CMD » au chef de mission diplomatique. Enfin, les cinq derniers chiffres indiquent le numéro d’ordre du véhicule.
En résumé, les plaques d’immatriculation vertes fournissent trois informations : le code du pays ou de l’organisation, le statut diplomatique et le numéro d’ordre du véhicule. Voilà, vous devriez maintenant mieux identifier ces plaques et les déchiffrer.

articles.title: Moteur Direct Drive et fonction vapeur : Xiaomi dégaine le lave-linge Mijia suréquipé à 349 €
articles.text:
Moteur Direct Drive et fonction vapeur : Xiaomi dégaine le lave-linge Mijia suréquipé à 349 €
Xiaomi commercialise le lave-linge Mijia Front Load Washer 7kg au tarif agressif de 349,00 €. Cet appareil à chargement frontal associe un format compact à une efficacité énergétique A-20 %, le tout pilotable via l'application Xiaomi Home et les assistants vocaux compatibles.
La grande offensive de Xiaomi sur le marché du gros électroménager français se poursuit. En effet, après l'annonce du réfrigérateur américain side-by-side MRS62ESSMPAEU et du lave-linge séchant WD080MJA08EU (entre autres), la déferlante continue avec le lave-linge gain de place Mijia WM070MJA07EU. Ce modèle se distingue de la concurrence grâce à sa profondeur de 45 cm qui permet de le placer là où des lave-linge de dimension standard (60 cm de profondeur) ne rentreraient pas forcément.
Un gabarit étroit et des caractéristiques techniques complètes
ON l'a dit, l'idée est bien sûr de gagner de l'espace et de séduire une clientèle majoritairement urbaine, dont les foyers se composent d'un couple avec un enfant, mais pas plus. En effet, la charge de linge maximale ne dépasse pas 7 en raison de la taille limitée du tambour qui doit rentrer dans le corps principal de taille réduite. Néanmoins, le fabricant promet que le diamètre de ce fameux tambour atteint 52 cm afin de ne pas froisser le linge plus que de raison et que c'est un moteur Direct Drive qui l'entraîne à la vitesse maximale de 1200 tr/min. Si la grande majorité des lave-linge du commerce atteignent une vitesse d'essorage de 1400 tr/min, ils ne sont pas tous équipés de ce type de motorisation qui se veut plus durable, plus économe en énergie et plus silencieuse qu'un moteur à courroie classique.
La machine intègre un système de détection automatique de charge qui adapte précisément le volume d'eau et la durée de lavage au poids constaté ; une technologie déjà largement maîtrisée. La fiche technique évoque une fonction de mise en pause qui autorise l'ajout de linge en cours de cycle, dès lors que la température du tambour et le niveau d'eau restent dans les normes de sécurité. Encore une fois, de nombreux modèles proposent cette fonctionnalité.
Connectivité écosystème et traitements hygiéniques par la vapeur
Ce modèle propose une palette de plus de 30 programmes de soin du linge. Le panneau de commande tactile à écran couleur donne accès à 14 cycles de base, alors que 16 programmes complémentaires sont sélectionnables depuis l'application mobile Xiaomi Home. Car évidemment, le lave-linge Mijia Mijia WM070MJA07EU est appairable à un smartphone. Cerise sur le gâteau, l'appareil s'intègre à l'écosystème domotique avec un pilotage vocal via Google Assistant et Amazon Alexa, une option qui ressemble plus à un gadget qu'à un véritable ame changer. On préfère largement l'intégration d'un générateur de vapeur qui assure une élimination des bactéries à hauteur de 99,99 % (selon la fiche technique, bien sûr) tout en assouplissant les fibres textiles pour faciliter le repassage. Le mode Refresh Care cible les odeurs, les plis et les poussières fines sur un à trois vêtements, complété par l'option Refresh & Loosen qui prévient le froissement en fin de cycle. Comme d'habitude, l'entretien du lave-linge utilise un programme d'autonettoyage du tambour à haute température.
On le voit, le lave-linge Mijia WM070MJA07EU ne manque pas d'atouts pour séduire, au premier rang desquels un moteur sans courroie et des fonctionnalités vapeur. Et ce qui ne gâche rien, le tout est proposé pour un prix défiant toute concurrence : 349 € seulement au moment de sa sortie.

articles.title: Spinny files confidential IPO papers, eyes upto Rs 3,000 Cr
articles.text:
Spinny files confidential IPO papers, eyes upto Rs 3,000 Cr
In August, Spinny’s parent company Valuedrive Technologies converted from a private limited company into a public limited company.
Used-car marketplace Spinny has filed draft papers for an IPO with the Securities and Exchange Board of India through the confidential route, according to a news report by Moneycontrol.
Spinny is looking to raise Rs 2,500 crore to Rs 3,000 crore through the IPO, according to the news report.
Founded in 2015, Spinny is an online used-car retailing platform that aims to bring about transparency and convenience in car buying and selling. The Gurugram-headquartered company was founded by Niraj Singh, Mohit Gupta, and Ramanshu Mahaur.
Earlier in August, Spinny’s parent company Valuedrive Technologies converted from a private limited company into a public limited company.
The company did not answer the e-mail queries sent by YourStory.
According to Tracxn, the Sachin Tendulkar-backed firm was valued at $1.13 billion as of May 2025. It competes with listed company CarTrade, its unit CarWale, as well as CarDekho and ZigWheels.
Spinny reported a loss of Rs 423.8 crore in FY25 compared to a loss of Rs 590 crore in the previous year. Revenue from contracts with customers rose 24.9% to Rs 4,657 crore during the period.
The pre-owned car platform has 36 car hubs across 15 cities, including Delhi, Bengaluru, Mumbai, Pune, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kolkata, Ahmedabad, and Lucknow.

articles.title: Orange lance sa propre marketplace : des milliers de smartphone, consoles, TV mis en vente
articles.text:
Orange vient de lancer sa propre marketplace entièrement dédiée aux produits tech. On retrouve notamment sur cette plateforme de vente en ligne des smartphones reconditionnés, des consoles de jeu, des casques audio, des téléviseurs ou encore des montres connectées. L’opérateur téléphonique assure avoir mis en place des règles strictes pour garantir la fiabilité de la plateforme.
Orange lance sa propre marketplace entièrement dédiée aux produits tech
Ce mardi 22 septembre 2026, Orange a lancé sa propre marketplace intégrée à ses boutiques en ligne Orange et Sosh. Cette plateforme de vente en ligne présente huit catégories : « Promotions et bons plans », « Smartphones reconditionnés », « Accessoires mobile », « TV, image et son », « Montres et objets connectés », « Consoles et gaming », « Informatique et tablettes » et « Maison et domotique ». La plateforme propose par exemple une PS5 Slim Edition Digital blanche à 676,04 €, un iPhone 16 à 577,90 €, ou encore une TV TCL Smart TV 32S4K QLED Full HD à 181,49 €.
Orange indique que 8 000 références sont d’ores et déjà présentes sur la plateforme et qu’elle devrait en compter plus de 40 000 d’ici la fin de l’année. L’opérateur précise que la section dédiée aux téléphones propose 1 500 références de smartphones reconditionnés, dont certains seraient « jusqu’à 50 % moins chers » que des modèles neufs. Laetitia Orsini-Sharps, directrice Grand Public d’Orange France, explique que cette offre a pour objectif de : « mieux répondre aux nouveaux réflexes d’achat high-tech des Français ».
Orange assure avoir mis en place un cadre strict pour ses vendeurs
Orange assure avoir mis en place un cadre strict pour ses partenaires de vente, afin de « garantir la qualité et la fiabilité de cette offre », ainsi qu’une sélection rigoureuse de vendeurs « 100 % basés en Europe, qui doivent répondre à des critères exigeants ». L’opérateur précise que ceux-ci seront soumis à un suivi régulier de leurs performances et de la qualité de leurs prestations.
Il est possible d’accéder à la marketplace d’Orange de deux façons différentes : depuis l’onglet « Tech et accessoires » des sites orange.fr et sosh.fr, ou depuis les applications Orange et moi et MySosh.

articles.title: Un avion autonome réalise le tout premier vol transcontinental presque sans pilote aux États-Unis
articles.text:
Un Cessna Caravan a traversé les États-Unis, de la Californie à la Caroline du Nord, sans que son pilote de sécurité touche une seule fois aux commandes. Joby Aviation annonce le premier vol transcontinental entièrement autonome du pays, sur 5 148 kilomètres.
Alors certes, 
un pilote de sécurité occupait la cabine, puisque la FAA l'exige, mais il n'a donné aucune commande durant le trajet. Dans son communiqué du 18 septembre, Joby, qui a mis au point l'engin, précise que l'avion a réalisé seul toutes les phases du vol, du roulage à l'atterrissage. Gizmodo précise que l'opération s'est déroulée en une semaine et quatre étapes. Le Caravan a relié Concord, en Californie, à l'aéroport régional du comté de Dare, sur les Outer Banks de Caroline du Nord. Il aurait même conclu ce parcours par un petit clin d'œil à l'histoire de l'aéronautique, avec passage à basse altitude près du monument de Kitty Hawk, où Orville et Wilbur Wright ont réalisé en 1903 le premier vol motorisé de l'histoire.
Un avion seul aux commandes, sous double supervision humaine
Phoenix Deer Valley est l'un des aéroports d'aviation générale les plus fréquentés du pays. À Phoenix, le Caravan a modifié seul sa route en temps réel pour éviter des orages, selon Joby.
Tout au long de la traversée, des opérateurs installés à l'Autonomy Headquarters de Joby, en Californie, et sur la base aérienne de Shaw, en Caroline du Sud, ont supervisé l'appareil jusqu'à 3 738 kilomètres de distance. Un pilote à distance a tenu le rôle de commandant de bord, d'après Aviacionline. Il a mis à jour le plan de vol et échangé avec le contrôle aérien, tandis que le pilote de sécurité pouvait reprendre les commandes en cas d'urgence.
Le Caravan est un Cessna 208B Grand Caravan produit en série, que Joby a équipé de son système de vol autonome J208. Il a volé sous un certificat expérimental de la FAA pour la recherche et le développement.
Airbus travaille aussi sur la supervision humaine d'appareils autonomes. En juillet, on vous l'a expliqué dans la démonstration de son logiciel MARS Autonomy sur deux drones Primoco One 150, au salon ILA de Berlin. Airbus a conçu ce logiciel pour qu'un seul chef de mission supervise plusieurs drones à la fois.
La technologie de Xwing et ses débouchés
Xwing est une start-up américaine de pilotage autonome pour avions-cargos. Joby a racheté sa division autonomie en juin 2024 et annonce plus de 400 vols et 800 heures de vol automatisé avec la technologie de Xwing. Lors de l'exercice Agile Flag de l'US Air Force, un avion équipé de cette autonomie a livré des pièces détachées critiques 24 heures plus vite que la logistique conventionnelle, d'après Joby. Pendant l'exercice REFORPAC, des opérateurs installés à Guam ont piloté à distance des avions basés à Hawaï, à près de 6 400 kilomètres.
Joby est surtout connue pour son taxi volant électrique de quatre passagers. Cet appareil vole jusqu'à 322 kilomètres par heure, mais Aviacionline précise qu'il sera d'abord exploité avec un membre d'équipage à bord, avant que Joby ne lui applique la technologie de Xwing pour automatiser davantage le vol.
« Ce voyage à travers l'Amérique offre un aperçu d'une nouvelle ère de l'aviation », a indiqué JoeBen Bevirt, fondateur et P.-D.G de Joby. Il cite notamment la desserte de communautés isolées, ainsi que l'objectif de « garder les pilotes hors de danger ». Joby a aussi profité de l'escale sur la base de Shaw pour une démonstration de capacités.
Comme le précise TechCrunch, Joby compte d'abord commercialiser un avion régional équipé de son système autonome. Cet avion pourrait effectuer des missions de défense et transporter du fret commercial. Pour soutenir ce projet, l'US Air Force a signé un contrat de 17 millions de dollars avec l'entreprise. En août, Joby a en outre racheté Resonant Sciences pour 500 millions de dollars. Resonant Sciences fabrique des systèmes radiofréquences et des capteurs, dans l'Ohio.
Mais pour l'heure, aucune date de mises en commercialisation n'a été communiquée par Joby. Tout ce que l'entreprise laisse filtrer est que le Caravan repartira d'abord vers l'ouest, avec sept étapes prévues de Raleigh à Portland, dans l'Oregon.

articles.title: US and China propose hotline to de-escalate AI threats ahead of Washington summit
articles.text:
US and China propose hotline to de-escalate AI threats ahead of Washington summit — comms channel between both nations to be left open in case of national security threats posed by autonomous artificial intelligence
A red telephone for the 21st century.
The U.S. and China have proposed developing a hotline for AI incident reports to address the risk of a rogue AI model getting out of control and to prevent misinterpretations of attacks that could trigger rapid autonomous escalation, Reuters reports. This news comes ahead of a planned visit by Chinese Premier Xi Jinping to Washington on September 24. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also confirmed that follow-up AI safety discussions are scheduled between the two nations in two months' time.
All of this sits against the backdrop of ongoing U.S. China trade and relations talks, in addition to various frontier AI agents seemingly breaking out of their containment and hacking organizations without oversight from humans.
While some are raising the alarm about the humanitarian risk posed by AI models, the U.S. and China are taking steps to ensure that if either party does end up triggering a dangerous AI event, there may be the opportunity for a joint response from both nations ahead of any potential perceived threat or escalation.
As artificial intelligence continues to make headlines circling around safety, both the U.S. and China now appear to be building global safeguards through a dedicated hotline to discuss any AI-related issues that escalate to national security threats.
Keeping humans in the loop
Following discussions between Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York over the weekend, the two sides have proposed that President Trump and Xi Jinping discuss various AI safety mechanisms, including a notification system focused around national security. This could include warnings of detected rogue AI actors operating anywhere in the world, as well as informing the other partner if an autonomous system performed an action that could be misinterpreted as an attack.
The scenario both parties want to avoid is an AI-driven autonomous weapon system — be they kinetic or something more asymmetric in nature, like AI-driven cyber attack capabilities — responding to provocation without consideration by a human. That could then trigger an escalated response in another AI system, leading to rapid escalation to full-blown conflict at a pace where humans wouldn't be able to intervene.
The proposed system could also help both parties develop joint responses to positive goals, as well as potential threats. This could form the basis for joint development pacing, considering the recent calls from U.S. AI firms to slow AI development to improve alignment and safeguards. China is less keen, suggesting that such a move could be used to hamper Chinese AI developments.
It's not clear at this time how keen China is to implement the proposed notification system, but analysts and experts on both sides have called for a system like this to be developed. Both the U.S. and China have agreed to further broach AI safety concerns in the coming months.
Laying the groundwork
We're still in the very early days of these discussions, with only the bare bones of a proposal for a hotline in place, and much to discuss on alignment between the two major AI-developing countries. The next step will be the talks between the two leaders, where much more than AI will be discussed.
If the relationship between the U.S. and China can move beyond its ongoing rivalry, the potential is there for much firmer agreements on the specifics around AI integration in national security and military actions. Although some analysts remain sceptical of firm agreements because of the limited trust between the two parties, there is some hope that agreements can be made on the direct weaponization of AI, core principles of AI safeguarding, and preventing them from targeting or damaging critical infrastructure.
The hope for a successful meeting is very much bipartisan. Leading Democrat in the U.S. House, Representative Ro Khanna, said that the first thing President Trump and Xi Jinping should work on in their meeting is developing core AI principles. Particularly around banning recursive self-improving AI and removing the option to use such autonomous systems on biological and nuclear weapons technology.
Washington's summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping is scheduled to begin in just a few days, where much more will be discussed beyond AI safety, as the rest of the world waits with bated breath, as the meeting between the two leaders could set the stage for another round of discussions surrounding the two nations' economic relations.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: The AI advice gap: what happens when the machine says "yes"?
articles.text:
The AI advice gap: what happens when the machine says "yes"?
AI financial advice has no regulator, no safety net.
Ask a UK bank for investment advice, and you get a lawful recommendation. If it was negligent, you will have the right to make a claim using the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.
Ask ChatGPT, or, more fashionable, Claude, the same question and you get nothing. Just an answer, but it will be delivered with a more confident tone, no matter whether it's right or absolutely wrong.
Despite that, more than a quarter of UK consumers now say they trust AI chatbots for money advice. The Financial Conduct Authority found this figure and flagged it as a live concern in its most recent review.
Founder & Executive Director of B2PRIME Group.
Other surveys found even higher figures. STRAT7 found 55% of UK adults have used AI for financial guidance, Sky News reported 40%, and EY's global study measured Gen Z adoption at 68%. Whatever the precise number is, the direction is the same.
People have started to trust AI more and more in their financial decisions. But the debate about it has, so far, been asking the wrong question.
What is the wrong question?
Most publications today focus on accuracy, and what everyone wants to know is whether the AI's advice is good. But is it?
In one study, there were five real financial scenarios passed to major chatbots, and the output was compared to certified financial planners. The result was unsurprising, though. The bots reliably missed emotional and situational context, so personal decisions turned to rough spreadsheet logic that missed important input.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Sky News has conducted a similar test, where three chatbots were given £16,000 in real savings. What they found was that the recommendations were US-biased and incomplete.
Most alarming, it was an investigation which found Claude incorrectly described Binance as FCA-registered when advising a beginner on cryptocurrency. Binance was, in fact, ordered to cease UK-regulated activity back in 2021.
AI’s misleading outputs sound disturbing, but what is even worse is that it is only one part of the problem. Things get harder after the incorrect advice has already been given, acted on, and gone wrong.
So, when it happens, who takes the blame? Nobody is the answer, although it’s quite uncomfortable to hear.
The FCA has noted the same. In its 2026 report, the regulator confirmed that LLM platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude sit entirely outside its regulatory remit. This means that consumers using them for financial guidance are not receiving regulated advice. Therefore, they have no access to the Financial Ombudsman Service (or the Financial Services Compensation Scheme) if things go wrong.
That said, the safety net simply does not apply the moment consumers paste a question into a chatbot.
The regulatory gap explained
To understand why this gap exists, let’s understand how UK financial regulation actually works. The regulatory perimeter is activity-based, not technology-based. This means what matters most is what is being done, not how.
A firm that provides personalized recommendations on the purchase, sale, or holding of certain assets is engaged in regulated activity, regardless of whether those recommendations are provided by a person or an algorithm.
The problem is that AI chatbots occupy a new space. They are not marketed as financial advisers, so they don't claim to be regulated. And technically, in most cases, they are not offering advice in the strict legal sense — they are responding to open questions.
Again, this ambiguity was addressed in the FCA report. The Mills Review highlights that AI platforms may influence consumers’ financial decisions without clearly implementing regulated actions. As a consequence, this creates a serious blank space between the actual financial impact and the protection provided by regulatory authorities.
The review's main recommendation was for the FCA to officially revise the scope for receiving financial recommendations developed using AI tools. So, this process is ongoing, and further updates will be available only after a few months, or even more.
The consumer protection problem and what fintech can do
While there is no law so far protecting ordinary people, what should we do? Can fintechs close this gap, at least for now?
First of all, waiting for the FCA perimeter check to be completed is not a strategy. It’s better to start by separating information from personalization, especially if your company has an AI assistant.
The thing is that the boundaries of recommendations depend on whether the conclusion is adapted to the specific circumstances of a particular person. The tool that generally explains what an ETF is is in a completely different regulatory status than the one that says how much you should invest in funds.
Also, make sure the disclaimer does real work. The footer text “not financial advice,” located below a specific recommendation, will not pass regulatory checks. The FCA evaluates content, not form. If the output data looks like a personalized recommendation, the tiny disclaimers will not reclassify it.
Although many people use AI today, do not overuse it to earn trust. An analysis of more than 330 million reviews showed that mentions of interaction with AI are rated, on average, at just 1.7 points, compared to 3.7 points for reviews that do not mention AI.
Final words
Surely, there will be some people who continue to use AI directly for financial advice, and their number will grow. For them, I can say only one thing: be careful about who you trust with your earnings. If no one is accountable, maybe not treating it as a rulebook will save you from losses.
But fintechs should start building the accountable version of their business, with an audit trail and a human above the AI layer. So when the machine says "yes," someone is actually standing behind that answer.

articles.title: Le Rampart, la nouvelle arme anti-drones de la Marine nationale, repéré sur le Mistral avant son départ pour l'Afrique
articles.text:
C’est un équipement militaire nouveau dans les forces armées françaises, qui pourrait bien être généralisé s’il fait ses preuves lors des exercices qui lui seront soumis. Sur des photos diffusées par des comptes dédiés aux sujets militaires, une tourelle inhabituelle a été repérée sur le pont du Mistral, l’un des trois porte-hélicoptères amphibies de la Marine nationale.
Il n’a pas fallu bien longtemps aux spécialistes pour identifier cette structure installée sur le navire. Ce module est appelé Rampart : il s’agit du nouveau nom, plus spectaculaire et plus symbolique, pour désigner le lanceur modulaire polyvalent (LMP), un projet d’armement porté par Naval Group, l’un des géants de la défense en Europe.
Cette nouvelle identité, officialisée en juin au salon Eurosatory, peut toutefois faire perdre de vue l’objectif de cette initiative : disposer d’une tourelle polyvalente, capable d’accueillir des modules spécifiques pour des munitions variées. L’idée ? Avoir un seul élément capable de gérer à la volée des menaces différentes nécessitant des intercepteurs précis.
Ce printemps, un démonstrateur avait déjà tiré à Canjuers (Var), le plus grand camp militaire d’Europe occidentale, notamment des roquettes de 68 mm (guidées laser et non guidées) « dans une configuration sol-sol ». Naval Group, satisfait de cette première vague de tests, ajoutait que l’étape suivante passerait par des « essais en mer ».
Un baptême du feu en mer dans le golfe de Guinée
C’est ce qui semble se concrétiser aujourd’hui. RFI rapportait d’ailleurs, dès le 13 septembre, le prochain appareillage d’un porte-hélicoptères amphibie en direction du golfe de Guinée, au large de l’Afrique de l’Ouest, dans le cadre de la mission récurrente Corymbe. Le 14, Le Marin indiquait que le PHA en partance était bien le Mistral, celui équipé du Rampart.
D’ailleurs, Naval Group avait annoncé un premier tir en mer en octobre, à bord d’un Mistral. On parlait alors d’un essai dans le cadre de l’exercice Wildfire, exercice spécifiquement pensé à la lutte intensive anti-drones, dont la date pour l’édition 2026 n’a pas été indiquée.
Si le Rampart voyage avec le Mistral, ce n’est certainement pas un hasard : le constructeur entend profiter manifestement de ce déploiement pour l’éprouver en mer – la fameuse prochaine étape de la campagne de tirs, qui implique de nouveaux scénarios, comme faire face à des drones navals et à des menaces aériennes diverses.
Le Rampart est capable d’aligner des munitions comme des roquettes, des missiles, des grenades, des leurres et même des armes sous-marines et des drones. Sa capacité d’autodéfense rapprochée est annoncée jusqu’à huit kilomètres (et même jusqu’à dix kilomètres, avance Mer et Marine), avec le soutien d’une tonne de projectiles à bord (la « charge utile »).
L’équation économique face aux menaces asymétriques
Le lanceur modulaire polyvalent entend apporter une réponse au « contexte actuel de menaces asymétriques et protéiformes », qui met à mal la logique plus traditionnelle d’un lanceur par type d’arme. La place croissante que les drones prennent dans la guerre, le développement des essaims et l’essor de l’IA embarquée imposent de repenser la défense.
Dans le jargon militaire, Rampart appartient à la famille des systèmes de défense rapprochée (CIWS, pour Close-In Weapon Systems), ces armes de dernier recours censées stopper une attaque juste avant l’impact (le nom de Rampart, rempart en français, colle donc plutôt bien à la fonction). Et le raisonnement derrière est d’abord comptable.
En mer Rouge, la marine américaine a passé des mois à abattre des drones houthis à quelques milliers d’euros pièce en y consacrant des missiles bien plus chers que leurs cibles, un échange intenable sur la durée. Même chose d’ailleurs pour la Marine nationale ainsi que pour les autres forces navales qui ont abattu des drones adverses.
Naval Group vend justement une proposition adaptée et à bas coût : une réponse « proportionnée au coût de la menace », autrement dit une roquette bon marché pour un drone bon marché. Pour garnir la tourelle, le groupe s’appuie sur Thales et KNDS, et travaille avec MBDA sur les missiles des familles Mistral et Akeron.
Un gain de puissance de feu pour la flotte française
Un LMP comme le Rampart vient par ailleurs muscler très franchement le Mistral, dont l’armement est léger. On ne compte que 2 canons de 20 mm téléopérés, 4 mitrailleuses de 12,7 mm, et 2 systèmes d’autodéfense surface-air à très courte portée SIMBAD (missile Mistral). Certes, le PHA est censé compter sur son escorte… mais faut-il encore qu’elle soit au niveau.
De fait, le LMP a de quoi partiellement compenser ce défaut d’escorte ; dans une zone où les drones se banalisent, ce type de configuration trouve tout son intérêt – même si le golfe de Guinée n’est pas reconnu pour être une zone très chaude en matière de drones kamikazes, contrairement au Moyen-Orient ou bien au théâtre ukrainien.
Au-delà des trois PHA de la Marine nationale, le Rampart pourrait aussi être étendu à d’autres navires d’importance, comme des frégates de premier rang, particulièrement exposés, mais aussi des navires très stratégiques, tels le porte-avions Charles de Gaulle et son successeur (le France Libre, qui accueillera aussi des systèmes laser).

articles.title: 22 Staaten fordern globale KI-Behörde – ausgerechnet USA und China nicht dabei
articles.text:
22 Staaten fordern globale KI-Behörde – ausgerechnet USA und China nicht dabei
Angesichts rasanter technologischer Fortschritte und jüngster Sicherheitsvorfälle dringt eine Gruppe von 22 Staats- und Regierungschefs auf eine schärfere internationale Aufsicht über besonders leistungsfähige Systeme Künstlicher Intelligenz. Eine am Rande der Generalversammlung der Vereinten Nationen in New York vorgestellte Erklärung verlangt verbindliche Sicherheitsregeln für Entwickler sowie den Aufbau einer weltweiten Kontrollbehörde nach dem Vorbild internationaler Aufsichtsorganisationen.
Zu den Erstunterzeichnern des Aufrufs gehören neben den Initiatoren aus Finnland und Norwegen auch Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) sowie die Präsidentin der Europäischen Kommission, Ursula von der Leyen. Bürgerrechtler kritisieren das Vorhaben hingegen als zu zögerlich und fordern stattdessen harte Strafen gegen die Führungskräfte führender Technologie-Unternehmen.
Sorge vor Kontrollverlust über selbstständige KI-Programme
Auslöser des diplomatischen Vorstoßes, der maßgeblich vom finnischen Präsidenten Alexander Stubb und dem norwegischen Regierungschef Jonas Gahr Støre vorangetrieben wurde, sind Berichte über besorgniserregende Fähigkeiten neuester Computerprogramme. In der Erklärung heißt es, man habe zuletzt beobachten müssen, wie hochleistungsfähige Systeme eingebaute Schutzvorkehrungen umgingen, Sicherheitslücken ausnutzten und unbefugten Zugriff auf reale Computernetze erlangten.
Führende Forscher und Unternehmenschefs warnten bereits davor, dass das Entwicklungstempo die menschliche Kontrollfähigkeit überholen könnte. Künstliche Intelligenz müsse daher zwingend unter menschlicher Leitung, Aufsicht und Kontrolle bleiben und im Einklang mit dem Völkerrecht stehen.
Drei-Punkte-Plan für weltweite KI-Schutzstandards
Das Papier formuliert drei zentrale Forderungen: Hersteller müssen nachvollziehbare Sicherheitsvorkehrungen treffen und unabhängigen Fachleuten vor der Freigabe neuer Programme umfassende Prüfungen ermöglichen. Zudem sollen Regierungen einheitliche Vorgaben schaffen und schwerwiegende Störfälle gegenseitig melden. Schließlich fordern die Unterzeichner die Staaten der Vereinten Nationen auf, den Aufbau einer weltweiten Einrichtung zu prüfen, die verbindliche Maßstäbe setzt, Kontrollen durchführt und Staaten zusammenruft, sobald bestimmte Leistungsgrenzen überschritten werden.
Neben europäischen Ländern haben sich unter anderem Australien, Kanada, Kenia, Singapur und Südafrika angeschlossen. Die technologisch führenden Mächte USA und China fehlen bislang.
Bürgerrechtler fordern persönliche Strafen für Konzernchefs
Deutliche Kritik an dem Vorstoß kommt von der Berliner Bürgerrechtsorganisation AlgorithmWatch, die vor zeitraubenden Scheinlösungen warnt. Man begrüße zwar das Bemühen, Gefahren für die Gesellschaft abzuwenden, sagte Geschäftsführer Matthias Spielkamp. Was die Politik jedoch übersehe, sei, dass man nicht die Beherrschung einer Technik verliere, sondern die Kontrolle über die Firmen, die sie herstellen. Ein weltweites Abkommen auszuhandeln, nehme Jahre in Anspruch, während die Konzerne unbeirrt weitermachen könnten.
Spielkamp sagte, die Europäische Union und die amerikanische Regierung könnten führende Anbieter schon heute in die Pflicht nehmen, wenn sie die bestehende europäische Gesetzgebung sowie bestehende Gesetze gegen Rechnerangriffe konsequent durchsetzen und Entwickler haftbar machen würden. Würden den Konzernchefs Haftstrafen oder ihren Unternehmen finanzielle Strafen in Milliardenhöhe drohen, wäre das verantwortungslose Vorgehen rasch beendet.

articles.title: Activision says the Call of Duty cheat economy is now a $8.5 billion industry
articles.text:
In context: Ahead of the much-awaited Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launch on October 22, Activision has published a detailed report on how the global video game cheat economy has evolved into a multi-billion-dollar business spanning subscription services, cheat reskins, illicit accounts, and spoofing hardware, supported by an organized network of hackers, resellers, and distributors.
The company also cited a recent study by threat intelligence firm Intorqa, which claims the cheat economy generates between $5.1 billion and $13.8 billion every year, with the median estimate being around $8.5 billion. The study claims that the cheat economy is made up of two revenue streams: subscription software and a wide network of supporting tools and services.
According to the research data, cheat subscriptions for just 15 popular titles generate around $3.5 billion per year, while account trading, boosting services, hardware ID spoofers, and other tools that are largely sold through organized distributor networks account for at least another $5 billion.
As part of its anti-cheat operations in collaboration with federal and local law enforcement agencies, Activision has reportedly disrupted 375 reseller operations, issued more than 80 cease-and-desist notices, and shut down 31 primary cheat vendors.
The company also recently released a video showing bodycam footage of an alleged Call of Duty cheat maker being served a cease-and-desist order at their Ohio residence.
 – Call of Duty (@CallofDuty) August 28, 2026
Due to the complexity, time, and cost involved in detecting and eliminating cheating in online multiplayer games, Activision says that its Ricochet Anti-Cheat technology does not try to catch one cheater at a time. Instead, it combines "detection, account security, TPM 2.0 enforcement, deep investigations, and legal action" to combat the cheating ecosystem.
The company added that it has adopted a multi-layered approach to counter cheating, whereby each layer targets one of the three pillars of the market: software- and hardware-based cheats, replacement accounts, and evasion tools such as spoofers. Activision is also working with law enforcement to dismantle distribution networks and catch the people operating them.
Explaining the scale and scope of the modern cheating economy, Activision noted that cheating tools include aimbots, wallhacks, rage cheats, unlock tools, DMA-based cheating hardware, and external devices designed to manipulate gameplay, such as Cronus, XIM, and Titan.
Account theft has also become big business, with one out of three gamers reporting that their accounts were hacked within the last two years. According to Activision, the ongoing bans on cheating accounts have created a massive demand for stolen accounts, aged accounts, Ranked Play-ready accounts, and boosting services.
Hardware-based spoofers, evasion tools, and related services are also being sold as part of a thriving online ecosystem helping cheaters evade bans. Activision says it is using "behavioral and technical detections" to thwart spoofers, adding that it issued more than 70,000 new hardware bans in August as part of its ongoing fight against this practice.

articles.title: Cable Matters Introduces 40 Gbps USB4 KVM Switch for Two Laptops
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 22nd 2026
	
	
	
	
Cable Matters Introduces 40 Gbps USB4 KVM Switch for Two Laptops
Cable Matters introduces its 40 Gbps USB4 KVM Switch for two laptops, model 201342, designed to simplify workspaces shared by two computers. Users can switch a compatible USB-C monitor or docking station between laptops, giving the selected computer access to the connected display and peripherals without repeatedly moving cables.
Jeff Jiang, President of Cable Matters Inc."Switching between a work laptop and a personal computer should be simple. The new USB4 KVM switch lets users share a compatible monitor or docking station at the press of a button, making it easier to use both computers in one organized workspace."
The switch combines two built-in host cables and one built-in output cable in a compact enclosure. Users can select a computer with the onboard button or included RF remote control, which operates without a direct line of sight.
Rated capabilities include data rates up to 40 Gbps, video output up to 8K at 60 Hz, 6K at 60 Hz, or 4K at 240 Hz, and USB Power Delivery pass-through up to 140 W. Actual performance depends on the connected computer, monitor or dock, and other equipment. Charging power passes to the selected laptop only and depends on the power source and receiving computer.
Compatible with Thunderbolt 4 and Thunderbolt 5 equipment, the switch supports connections up to its 40 Gbps limit. A compatible docking station or monitor allows users to share its connected keyboard, mouse, storage, and other peripherals between computers, helping reduce duplicate equipment on the desk.
Compatible docking stations must have a detachable host cable. Docks with permanently attached host cables cannot be connected using a USB-C coupler, and USB-C extension cables are not supported. Video output requires a compatible host port with display support; a USB-C data-only port cannot provide video. Supported resolutions, refresh rates, and display configurations depend on the host computer and connected equipment.

iPhone 17e (512 GB) traz chip A19 de alto desempenho e câmera de 48 MP; celular acessível da Apple atinge o menor preço histórico com desconto de 34% com cupom
O iPhone 17e de 512 GB está saindo por R$ 4.799 no Pix com cupom INFLU300 no Magazine Luiza. O celular acessível da Apple, equipado com o chip A19 e uma câmera principal de 48 MP, alcança o menor preço histórico com desconto de 34% sobre o original de R$ 7.299.
Mesmo sendo o mais “baratinho” da Apple, o iPhone 17e oferece alto desempenho alinhado com os demais modelos da linha 2025, com o chip A19 (o mesmo do iPhone 17) e os 8 GB de RAM sustentando apps pesados e funções do Apple Intelligence. Seu painel Super Retina XDR OLED de 6,1″ possui um brilho de até 1.200 nits e reproduz imagens com cores vibrantes, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer ambiente. O vidro Ceramic Shield 2 protege o display contra pancadas e quedas.
O gadget conta com uma única câmera wide de 48 MP na traseira, que possui OIS e “zoom com qualidade óptica” de até 2x, que faz uso de algoritmos para realizar aproximações com alta resolução. A lente frontal de 12 MP tira ótimas selfies. Ambas filmam em 4K a 60 fps.

articles.title: AstroForge is putting AI in command of its next spacecraft | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Fly to an asteroid, land on it, make no mistakes: If only it were that easy.
When NASA sends spacecraft to explore the solar system, they build in redundancy and automation. But much of the work is done by teams of flight controllers communicating with the vehicle from Earth. The OSIRIS-REx mission, which rendezvoused with an asteroid in 2018, had 100 operators on each eight-hour shift.
But resources like that aren’t available to startups, so AstroForge, which is developing technology to mine asteroids, is turning to AI. The company has developed an autonomous control stack for its spacecraft called “Solo,” a transformer-based model made in-house.
AstroForge plans to fly its first autonomous spacecraft in 2027 on the first rocket launched by Stoke Space. That mission will be backed by NASA and is expected to gather scientific data about the sun.
That would be an accomplishment: Most spacecraft autonomy depends on traditional control algorithms due to concerns about the unreliability of neural networks. The first use of a neural network to control a satellite’s positioning in orbit took place just last year.
AstroForge, founded in 2022 and backed with $56 million in venture funding, has launched two prototype spacecraft, both of which suffered anomalies that prevented them from achieving most of their mission objectives. In 2025, its Odin spacecraft was launched into deep space, but the company had difficulty communicating with it. There are a limited number of antennas on Earth big enough to transmit to spacecraft hundreds of thousands of miles away, and the windows of time in which to do it are small.
Ultimately, AstroForge couldn’t gain control of Odin, but the experience spurred it to consider alternatives: Could it put sufficient intelligence onboard the spacecraft for it to solve its own problems?
“Would that have been recoverable with all the data on the spacecraft? I don’t know, but I can tell you nothing onboard tried it, and I would love something onboard to try if the spacecraft is unrecoverable at launch,” Matthew Gialich, AstroForge’s co-founder and CEO, said.
“The trade for me is: Do I go build my own ground network, which is going to cost [around] $200 million to put up five dishes around the world and then do operations on it, or do I try to remove it with a model?”
Armand Awad, AstroForge’s head of flight software, said the company decided to leverage the advances in transformer models driven by the frontier labs. It created a stack that includes traditional control algorithms, models trained on test data for specific subsystems like power generation or navigation, and an overall intelligence layer trained on about 2,500 sensors in the spacecraft.
“I’m not saying I’m going to make general spacecraft autonomy or general autonomy for the world,” Gialich said. “I’m making a constrained autonomy at a very low sensor input, following the basic training of a transformer model.”
In theory, the agent in control of the spacecraft will perform tasks like anomaly resolution. Awad imagines it realizing that it has lost track of its position in space, correlating a power anomaly to issues in its star tracker, and fixing the whole thing — “probably turning it on and off in this case.”
The company’s third vehicle, DeepSpace-2, is currently set to launch alongside Intuitive Machines’ third moon mission, expected to head for space by the end of 2026. Solo will be onboard that vehicle, flying in “shadow mode,” so AstroForge’s engineers can put it through its paces before the Autonomy-1 mission.
Will this truly be an AI agent operating an independent spacecraft?
“I don’t plan on flying radios that can receive from Earth on Autonomy-1,” Gialich said. “We have to go all in right now. The team’s probably going to talk me into it by the time we fly it. But right now, I’m telling them no radios.”

articles.title: The Beats 360 are fun headphones that you can mix and match
articles.text:
For the past couple of weeks, I’ve been using the Beats 360 for my flights and commutes, and I’m impressed by Beats’ newest and flashiest headphones ever.
The audio device is made to be used all the time, whether you’re at the gym or you’re out and about looking fancy. I really appreciate the customizable headphones; you’re able to swap out ear cups and headband cushion, so you can mix and match to your liking.
At first, I was a bit skeptical because I thought swapping would be a pain in the ass. In the past, when companies say that something is easy to swap out, I’ve found it usually isn’t quite so easy. But what I like about the Beats 360 is that they’re kind of idiot proof, and this is what I need: idiot-proof customization options, and I’m pleased.
With a twist, the cups pop off the headphones, and another twist helps you put new colours in. At the top, the headband has little holes on the underside that make it easy to clip the cushion into it. They’re so easy to remove that another tech creator just snatched an earcup when I was wearing the headphones around my neck.
Now, swappable cups alone wouldn’t be exciting, except Beats lets you mix and match colours, and that’s pretty dope. The headphones come in Black, Cloud, Sky and Pink, and of course these all have matching pieces, but there’s also ‘Spark,’ which is like a neon yellow, and Navy, giving you tons of colours to mix and match. There are also leather options in Black and Cloud as well for a night out on the town. My favourite combination is the Black headset with Spark.
The Beats 360 are IPX4 and come with ‘Performance Knit’ cups that allow you to sweat in the earbuds without damaging them. And if your workout is intense, you can easily swap out the cups or the headband cushion. I’m a pretty sweaty dude, so I was able to see that the cups dealt pretty well with sweat.
The Beats 360 feel okay on your head. They’re comfortable after you start wearing them for a while. At least I found the top band a bit tight on my head, but after wearing them for 20 minutes, this feeling goes away. The Performance Knit cushions also use plush memory foam, which might explain why it starts to feel better after some time. Maybe the shape of my head is weird because I found the AirPods Max headphones more comfortable, which people tend to complain about. But the degree of comfort isn’t that bad at all. For instance, I wore them on a seven-hour flight straight, and even fell asleep while wearing them.
The Beats 360 sound great; Beats said they improved the active noise cancellation from the Beats Studio. It’s pretty good at shutting out most noise without needing to raise the volume too loud. Airplane and subway sounds disappear completely; however, the high-pitched sound of a baby crying made it through. The baby was an aisle over on a two-aisle plane, but it wasn’t like I could 100 per cent tell what I was hearing at first. I just thought it was a sound in the background of my show. I was watching Secret Lives of Mormon Wives; all these women have babies, but when I removed the headphones, it was like, “Oh, this baby isn’t on my show, and is pretty loud.”
The Beats 360 offers rich sound with immersive audio. I played music and watched media for hours, and it all sounds great. It also has Adaptive EQ, which adjusts acoustic frequencies based on the fit. Plus, there’s Personalized Spatial Audio with head tracking and Dolby Atmos, with a built-in accelerometer and gyroscope for head tracking.
When I was testing audio, I picked songs like Middle Child by J.Cole, Another One Bites the Dust by Queen, Humble by Kendrick Lamar, and We Are Young, which are pretty different songs, but also the same ones I used to test Apple’s AirPods Max 2. It’s pretty interesting comparing the two headphones; both sound good and are immersive. Strangely, I think the Beats 360 are even louder than the AirPods Max 2, but loudness isn’t everything.
I found that Middle Child had a bit of a punch to the bass that was a little bit overwhelming (though I was playing the music at the loudest volume to compare), which isn’t something I hear with the AirPods Max 2. Other songs like Another One Bites the Dust and Humble sounded very similar on the two headsets; voices are clear and precise, so you can hear harmonies very well. For instance, there’s a very quiet harmony in We Are Young that’s slightly delayed, like an echo, that I can hear pretty well between both headsets.
However, the experience between the two headphones for We Are Young is interesting. I think the instrumentals are stronger on the AirPods Max 2, as it feels like We Are Young is a huge production, whereas on the Beats 360, you can hear a lot, but it sounds a bit lacking. But again, I definitely needed to keep the volume on max to hear the difference.
One thing I found a little weird: when you take off the headphones, your media doesn’t auto-pause. Also, the Beats 360 work on both Android and iOS, but you need to download the Beats app on Android, while on iOS, it just works and you can control the headphones via your settings, similar to any AirPods.
I enjoyed the Beats 360 headphones, but definitely my favourite thing was the customizable cushions and the variety of colours they come in. Although I noted that there weren’t any red options, which feels like a miss considering it’s Beats. The Beats 360 costs $479.95, and the cushion kit costs $74.95. However, until October 31, you can grab different cushion kits for $14.99, which I think is a sick introductory offer that I might take advantage of — I love mixing and matching.
